chapters.title: Marketing: Core Concepts, Philosophies and the Marketing Mix
chapters.scope: What marketing is, how the idea of it has changed, and the mixes (4Ps, 4Cs, 4As) used to plan it.

blocks.title: What marketing is
blocks.html:
A small firm in Pune makes a good water purifier, but sales are slow, and the owners' first idea is to push the sales team harder. Marketing starts a step earlier: what do buyers need, and what will they pay for?

In plain wordsMarketing is finding out what people need and want, and offering them something they value, at a profit.

Exam definitionMarketing is “the activity, set of institutions, and processes for creating, communicating, delivering, and exchanging offerings that have value for customers, clients, partners, and society at large” (American Marketing Association, definition approved 2017).

Philip Kotler calls marketing the social and managerial process by which individuals and groups obtain what they need and want through creating and exchanging products and value with others. Kotler and Keller's shortest definition is “meeting needs profitably”.

ConceptMeaningExample
NeedA state of felt deprivation: basic requirements such as food, safety and belongingHunger
WantThe form a need takes, shaped by culture and individual personalityA dosa, or a burger
DemandA want backed by the ability and willingness to payBuying a ₹120 dosa at a restaurant

Needs may be physical (food, clothing, shelter), social (belonging, affection, recognition) or individual (knowledge, self-expression). Take thirst: the need is to quench it, the want is water, and the demand is a particular brand of bottled water the buyer can pay for.

Exchange. Marketing works through exchange. A transaction is one completed exchange.

AspectExchangeTransaction
MeaningThe process of obtaining a desired product from someone by offering something of value in returnA trade of values between two parties, the unit of exchange
InvolvesAt least two parties, each with something the other values, free to accept or rejectAt least two things of value, agreed conditions, a time and a place
ExampleBarterA purchase, or a banking transaction

Utility. A buyer agrees to an exchange because they expect satisfaction from the product's utility: the value that makes it able to satisfy a want. Marketing adds several kinds. A dealer who delivers a refrigerator to a village adds place utility; an EMI plan that spreads the payment adds possession utility.

UtilityValue added by…
FormTurning materials into a usable product; created mainly by production, guided by marketing research
PlaceMaking the product available where buyers want it
TimeMaking it available when they want it
PossessionTransferring ownership, helped by credit and easy payment
InformationTelling buyers that the product exists and what it does

What can be marketed. Ten kinds of entity, not only goods:

EntityExamples
GoodsPackaged foods, cars, phones
ServicesAirlines, banking, repairs; many offers, such as a restaurant meal, mix goods and services
EventsTrade shows, sporting events, festivals
ExperiencesTheme parks, river rafting, bungee jumping
PersonsArtists, performers, sportspeople, politicians
PlacesCities, states and countries: ‘Incredible India’, Kerala's ‘God's Own Country’
PropertiesReal estate, financial property such as shares
OrganisationsCompanies, universities, the armed forces recruiting
InformationEncyclopaedias, data, maps
IdeasSocial causes and new practices, such as digital payments

Don't confuse marketing with selling. Marketing is sometimes described as the art of selling. Peter Drucker argued the opposite: the aim of marketing is to know and understand the customer so well that the product fits and sells itself, which makes selling superfluous. Nor is a want the same as a need: marketers shape wants, but the need was there first.

Where it breaks. The definitions describe marketing at its best. Firms also use it to sell things people do not need, and the line between shaping wants and manipulating them is a judgement. The societal marketing concept, below, takes this up.

For exams. Expect the need–want–demand chain, a kind of utility matched to an example, and the AMA or Kotler definition. Know Drucker's point that marketing aims to make selling superfluous.

Need, want plus buying power, demand.

blocks.title: States of demand
blocks.html:
In December a hotel in a hill station is full and turns guests away; in July it is half empty. The same hotel needs two different marketing jobs in one year.

In plain wordsA state of demand describes how much buyers want a product, and when, compared with what the seller can supply or wants to sell.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition, after Kotler: marketing management is demand management, influencing the level, timing and composition of demand so that the organisation reaches its objectives.

So marketers manage demand, not just respond to it. Philip Kotler (1973) described eight states of demand, each calling for a different marketing task.

StateSituationMarketing task
Negative demandMuch of the market dislikes the product and may even pay to avoid it, as with vaccinations or dental workConversional marketing: find out why, and change attitudes through redesign, lower prices or promotion
No demandBuyers are unaware of the product or uninterested in itStimulational marketing: connect the product's benefits to people's needs
Latent demandA strong need exists that no existing product satisfies, as for a truly affordable electric carDevelopmental marketing: measure the potential market and develop the product
Declining demandBuyers are buying less, or moving to newer productsRemarketing: reverse the decline with new markets, features or communication
Irregular demandPurchases vary by season, day or hour, as with raincoats or mosquito repellentSynchromarketing: smooth demand with flexible pricing and promotion
Full demandBuyers are buying all the products put on the marketMaintenance marketing: keep quality up and watch satisfaction
Overfull demandMore buyers want the product than can be satisfied, as with train tickets in the holiday seasonDemarketing: reduce demand temporarily, for example by raising prices or cutting promotion
Unwholesome demandThe product has undesirable social consequences, as with tobaccoCountermarketing: persuade people to give it up, through warnings, high prices or reduced availability

Back to the hill-station hotel. Its demand is irregular, so its task is synchromarketing. It might offer lower monsoon tariffs and promote off-season events to fill July rooms. In peak weeks it can raise tariffs, which also eases the pressure of overfull demand.

Don't confuse demarketing with countermarketing. Demarketing cuts demand for a wanted product for a while, because supply cannot keep up. Countermarketing tries to end demand for a harmful product. Likewise, latent demand is a need with no product to meet it; no demand is a product that buyers do not care about.

Where it breaks. Real markets mix states. One product can face full demand in cities and no demand in villages, and the state changes over time. The eight states describe a market at one moment, so the task must be reviewed as the market moves.

For exams. Expect a state matched to its task. The pairs most often mixed up: irregular with synchromarketing, declining with remarketing, negative with conversional, latent with developmental.

Negative, none, latent, declining, irregular, full, overfull, unwholesome.

blocks.title: How marketing philosophies evolved
blocks.html:
A bicycle maker improves its frames every year, yet young buyers move to electric scooters. It perfected the product while the need it served, getting around town, found a new answer.

In plain wordsA marketing philosophy is the belief that guides a firm: whether it starts from its factory, its product, its sales push, or its customers and society.

Exam definitionThe marketing concept holds that achieving organisational goals depends on knowing the needs and wants of target markets and delivering the desired satisfactions better than competitors do (Kotler and Armstrong).

Six philosophies are usually taught, roughly in the order in which they appeared.

ConceptBeliefFocus
ProductionConsumers prefer products that are widely available and cheapEfficient production and wide distribution
ProductConsumers prefer the best quality, performance and featuresContinuous product improvement; risks ‘marketing myopia’
SellingConsumers will not buy enough unless persuadedAggressive selling and promotion of what the firm makes
MarketingThe key is to know the target market's needs and satisfy them better than competitorsCustomer needs: ‘sense and respond’ rather than ‘make and sell’
Societal marketingThe firm should also serve consumers' and society's long-term well-beingCompany profit, consumer wants and society's interests together
Holistic marketingEverything matters; the business is one connected systemBreadth and interdependence of all marketing activity

Marketing myopia (Theodore Levitt, 1960) is defining a business by its product rather than by the need it meets. The railways did this by seeing themselves in the railroad business rather than in transport. The bicycle maker above made the same mistake.

Levitt also drew the contrast between selling and marketing. Selling focuses on the seller's need to turn products into cash; marketing focuses on the buyer's needs. Selling works inside-out, from the factory; marketing works outside-in, from the market.

AspectSellingMarketing
EmphasisThe productCustomers' needs and wants
SequenceMake the product first, then work out how to sell itFind out what customers want, then design the product to satisfy it
ProfitFrom sales volumeFrom customer satisfaction and keeping customers over the long run
ViewpointThe seller's needsThe buyer's needs

Holistic marketing (Kotler and Keller) has four components:

  • Relationship marketing: lasting ties with customers, employees and partners.
  • Integrated marketing: all activities combined to create, communicate and deliver value.
  • Internal marketing: hiring, training and motivating staff to serve customers well, from top management down.
  • Performance marketing: financial returns, and the wider ethical, social and environmental effects.

Earlier editions named the fourth socially responsible marketing, a label many study notes still use.

Don't confuse societal marketing with holistic marketing. Societal marketing adds society's long-term well-being to consumer wants and company profit. Holistic marketing is wider: it treats all marketing activity as one connected system, and social responsibility is one part of it, under performance marketing.

Where it breaks. The six concepts are often taught as eras, one replacing the next. In fact all six exist today. Many firms still follow the production or selling concept, and selling is common for unsought goods such as insurance.

In practice. Ask where a plan starts. If it starts from stock in the warehouse and asks how to move it, it follows the selling concept. If it starts from a customer group and its needs, it follows the marketing concept.

Production, product, selling, marketing, societal, holistic.

blocks.title: The marketing mix: 4Ps, 4Cs and 4As
blocks.html:
A firm launches a good shampoo at a fair price, but the shops near its buyers do not stock it and few people have heard of it. One weak tool can sink the other three.

In plain wordsThe marketing mix is the handful of things a firm controls, chiefly its product, price, place and promotion, set together for one group of buyers.

Exam definitionThe marketing mix is the set of tactical marketing tools, product, price, place and promotion, that the firm blends to produce the response it wants in the target market (Kotler and Armstrong).

Neil Borden popularised the term (his 1964 article describes using it from 1949); E. Jerome McCarthy (1960) grouped the tools into the 4Ps. Robert Lauterborn (1990) restated them from the customer's side as the 4Cs. Jagdish Sheth and Rajendra Sisodia offered the 4As, also from the buyer's viewpoint.

4Ps (seller)4Cs (Lauterborn)4As (Sheth and Sisodia)
ProductCustomer solution (value)Acceptability: does it meet the customer's functional and psychological needs?
PriceCustomer costAffordability: are customers able and willing to pay?
PlaceConvenienceAccessibility: can customers readily get it?
PromotionCommunicationAwareness: do customers know about it and what it does?

An example. Take a shampoo maker aiming at village households, as an illustration. Product: a single-use sachet. Price: say ₹5, small enough to pay from a day's wages. Place: the village kirana store. Promotion: a wall painting and a demonstration at the weekly market. Read from the buyer's side, each P passes one A: the shampoo works (acceptable), the sachet is affordable, the store is a short walk away (accessible), and the demonstration makes people aware.

Services add three more Ps (people, process and physical evidence), covered in the services chapter.

Don't confuse the 4Cs with the 4As. Both look from the buyer's side. Lauterborn's 4Cs rename each P: price, for instance, becomes the customer's whole cost, not only the money. Sheth and Sisodia's 4As are tests the offer must pass with customers: acceptable, affordable, accessible and known.

Where it breaks. The 4Ps are a seller's checklist. They say nothing about which customers to serve; that comes first, from segmentation and targeting. The tools also interact: a deep price cut can undo a premium image that promotion has built.

For exams. Match each framework to its author: Borden (the term), McCarthy (4Ps, 1960), Lauterborn (4Cs, 1990), Sheth and Sisodia (4As). Expect a P matched to its C or A.

Go deeper for practitioners

Where the idea came from. Borden credited James Culliton (1948), who described the business executive as a “mixer of ingredients”. Borden's own list was much longer than four, with twelve elements such as branding, packaging, display and servicing. McCarthy's 4Ps made it short enough to teach and remember. Bernard Booms and Mary Jo Bitner (1981) added the three service Ps.

A decision. A two-wheeler tyre maker is losing sales in small towns. The sales team asks for a price cut. Research shows that local mechanics, whom riders trust, recommend a rival. That is a place-and-promotion problem, so a price cut would cost margin and leave the cause untouched. Working with mechanics is the better first move.

Links. Each P has its own chapter in this unit: product decisions, pricing decisions, distribution, and promotion decisions.

Product, price, place, promotion, seen from the buyer's side.

blocks.title: Forces reshaping marketing
blocks.html:
A neighbourhood electronics shop finds customers checking prices on their phones at the counter. Its pricing, service and stock all have to change, though nothing inside the shop has.

Kotler and Keller name the major societal forces that keep changing what marketers must do. A strategy that is not revised as these forces change soon loses its relevance.

ForceWhat it means
Network information technologyThe digital revolution allows more accurate production, more targeted communication and more relevant pricing
GlobalisationCheaper transport and communication let firms sell in, and consumers buy from, almost any country
Deregulation and privatisationOpening industries to competition, and turning public companies over to private ownership
Heightened competitionDomestic and foreign brands compete hard, raising marketing costs and shrinking margins
Industry convergenceIndustry boundaries blur, as computing and consumer electronics have merged
Retail transformationStores compete with TV shopping and e-commerce, and respond by selling an experience
DisintermediationOnline sellers bypass traditional channels; traditional firms respond with re-intermediation, becoming ‘brick-and-click’ rather than ‘pure-click’
Consumer buying power, information and participationBuyers compare prices and features anywhere, at any time, find information in depth, and influence peers and public opinion
Consumer resistanceSeeing fewer real differences between products, buyers are less loyal, more price- and quality-sensitive, and less tolerant of unwanted marketing

Back to the electronics shop. It faces several forces at once. Online sellers bypass it (disintermediation), and buyers arrive knowing the online price (consumer buying power). If it adds its own website and home delivery, it becomes a brick-and-click shop: that is re-intermediation.

New capabilities. The same forces give marketers new tools:

  • the internet as an information and sales channel with worldwide reach;
  • richer data about markets and individual customers;
  • social media and brand communities to amplify messages and buzz;
  • permission-based ads, coupons and samples;
  • mobile, location-based marketing near the point of sale;
  • mass customisation of products;
  • online recruiting, training and internal communication;
  • cost savings from comparing suppliers online and running reverse auctions.

Don't confuse disintermediation with re-intermediation. Disintermediation removes the middleman: the buyer deals with the seller directly online. Re-intermediation is the traditional firm's reply: it adds online channels of its own, so a pure-click rival meets a brick-and-click one.

Where it breaks. A list of forces dates quickly, and textbook editions regroup them. Use it as a checklist to scan, not as a fixed set. The forces also pull in different directions: technology makes mass customisation possible, while competition pushes prices down.

In practice. When reviewing a marketing plan each year, ask which force has moved most, and which part of the mix must change in response.

Technology, globalisation and empowered buyers keep changing the task.

text: The Kuṟaḷ says the proper trade of traders is to guard the interests of others as their own. The marketing concept rests on the same reversal of view, from what the seller wants to sell to what the buyer needs.

chapters.title: Segmentation, Targeting and Positioning
chapters.scope: How a firm divides a market, chooses whom to serve, and earns a distinct place in their minds.

blocks.title: Market segmentation
blocks.html:
A bank branch in a college town offers one savings account to students, retired teachers and shop owners. Students want a zero balance, retired teachers want safety and a helpful clerk, and shop owners want quick cash deposits. One account cannot please all three.

In plain wordsSegmentation is splitting a market into groups of buyers who want similar things, so that each group can get an offer that fits it.

Exam definitionMarket segmentation is dividing a market into distinct groups of buyers who have different needs, characteristics or behaviour, and who might require separate products or marketing programmes (Kotler and Armstrong).

STP, segmentation, targeting and positioning, is the sequence at the heart of marketing strategy. Segmentation comes first.

Two ways to find segments. Start from descriptive characteristics (geographic, demographic, psychographic) and check whether the groups differ in needs or responses. Or start from behavioural responses (benefits sought, usage occasions, brands) and check whether each group has a distinct profile: do car buyers who want quality rather than a low price differ in age, income or lifestyle?

BasisVariables
GeographicCountry, region, state, city size, urban or rural, climate
DemographicAge, gender, income, education, occupation, family size and life cycle, religion
PsychographicLifestyle, personality, values and interests; lifestyle is often measured by activities, interests and opinions (the AIO approach of William Wells and Douglas Tigert, 1971)
BehaviouralOccasions (weddings, birthdays), benefits sought (quality, service, economy), user status (non-user, ex-user, first-time user), usage rate (light, heavy), loyalty status (none, medium, strong), readiness stage (unaware, aware, intending to buy), attitude to the product

Demographic variables are popular because they are linked to needs and easy to measure. Even a segment described by personality has to be linked back to demographics, to estimate its size and choose media. Psychographics adds psychology: people with the same demographics can have very different lifestyles and values.

Levels of segmentation run from one offer for everyone to one offer per person.

LevelApproachWhat it doesExample
MacroMass (undifferentiated) marketingMass production, distribution and promotion of one product for all buyers: ‘one size fits all’One advertisement for milk aimed at every household
MicroSegment marketingDifferent offers for large groups with similar wants, buying power and habitsTerm insurance plans for young earners
MicroNiche marketingA narrower group with distinct needs, often willing to pay a premiumLuxury watches and sports cars
MicroLocal marketingProgrammes tailored to the needs of local customers: cities, neighbourhoods, storesA neighbourhood bakery or florist
MicroIndividual marketingThe ultimate level: customised or one-to-one marketingA custom-made wedding dress; made-to-order car interiors

Business markets are segmented with a nested approach from Thomas Bonoma and Benson Shapiro (1983). It runs from demographic or firmographic variables (industry, company size, location) and operating variables (technology used, user status, customer capabilities) to purchasing approaches (purchasing policies, buying criteria, how buying is organised). Then come situational factors (urgency, order size) and the personal characteristics of the buyers.

Useful segments are measurable, substantial (large and profitable enough), accessible, differentiable (they respond differently) and actionable (the firm can design programmes for them). To illustrate the size test: a gym in Indore counts 4,000 working women aged 25 to 40 nearby. If 5% join at ₹1,500 a month, that is 200 members and ₹3 lakh a month.

Don't confuse segmentation with targeting. Segmentation describes the groups in a market; targeting chooses which of them to serve. Keep the bases apart too: usage rate and loyalty are behavioural variables, not demographic ones. The word micromarketing is used two ways. In the table above, every level below mass marketing is micro, as in Kotler and Keller. Kotler and Armstrong keep the word for local and individual marketing only.

Where it breaks. Segments drawn on paper may not behave differently. If every group responds the same way to price and promotion, separate programmes add cost without adding sales. Demographics are easy to measure but describe buyers rather than explain them; many marketers believe behavioural variables are the best starting point (Kotler and Armstrong).

For exams. Expect a variable to be matched to its basis, and the five tests of a useful segment.

Geographic, demographic, psychographic, behavioural.

blocks.title: Targeting
blocks.html:
An auto-parts maker in Pune can sell brake pads to car makers, to two-wheeler makers, or to repair garages. It cannot serve all three well at once, so it has to choose.

In plain wordsTargeting is deciding which of the segments you found are worth serving, and how many to take on.

Exam definitionMarket targeting is evaluating each market segment's attractiveness and selecting one or more segments to enter (Kotler and Armstrong).

Evaluating segments. Each segment is judged on three things:

  • its size and growth;
  • its structural attractiveness: competition, substitutes, and the power of buyers and suppliers;
  • its fit with the firm's objectives and resources.

For the Pune maker, garages may be the largest segment, but they are scattered and buy in small lots. Car makers buy in bulk but have strong bargaining power. The firm weighs both against its own capacity and skills.

Choosing a pattern. Having evaluated the segments, the firm chooses how to cover them.

PatternWhat the firm serves
Single-segment concentrationOne segment with one product
Selective specialisationSeveral unrelated segments, each attractive on its own
Product specialisationOne product sold to several segments
Market specialisationMany needs of one particular customer group, with several products
Full market coverageAll customer groups with all the products they need, by undifferentiated or differentiated marketing

Examples. A luxury watchmaker concentrates on one high-end segment. A maker of nuts and bolts that sells different types to car makers, electrical-equipment makers and builders practises product specialisation. A firm selling an assortment of products only to ice-cream makers practises market specialisation. Only very large firms, such as Hindustan Unilever, Nestlé or Coca-Cola in non-alcoholic drinks, can attempt full market coverage.

These five patterns follow Derek Abell (1980) and are used by Kotler and Keller. Seen as strategies, targeting runs from undifferentiated (mass) marketing, through differentiated (segmented) and concentrated (niche) marketing, to micromarketing.

Don't confuse product specialisation with market specialisation. Product specialisation sells one product to many customer groups, like the nuts and bolts. Market specialisation sells many products to one customer group, like everything an ice-cream maker buys.

Where it breaks. Concentration is risky: if the one segment shrinks or a strong rival enters, the firm has nothing to fall back on. Full coverage spreads effort across many offers and suits only the largest firms. Targeting also raises ethical questions when the chosen segment is vulnerable, such as children for sugary snacks.

In practice. Many firms start with one segment and add others over time, one by one, rather than entering all at once. For exams, expect a case matched to one of the five patterns, and the four strategies in order.

Evaluate the segments, then choose a pattern of coverage.

blocks.title: Positioning
blocks.html:
Two detergents clean equally well. Yet shoppers think of one as ‘the gentle one’ and the other as ‘the one for tough stains’. Each brand holds a place in buyers' minds, and that place decides many purchases.

In plain wordsPositioning is choosing the one idea you want buyers to link with your brand, then making the product and its messages fit that idea.

Exam definitionPositioning is the act of designing the company's offering and image to occupy a distinctive place in the minds of the target market (Kotler and Keller).

Al Ries and Jack Trout made the idea famous (Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind, 1981): positioning is not what you do to a product but what you do to the prospect's mind.

Points of difference and parity. A position rests on two kinds of association. This pairing is Kevin Lane Keller's.

TypeMeaningRole
Points of difference (PODs)Attributes or benefits that customers strongly associate with the brand, rate positively, and believe they could not find to the same extent in a competitorGive customers a reason to choose the brand
Points of parity (POPs)Associations that are not unique but are needed for the brand to be credible in its category, or that neutralise a competitor's points of differenceRemove reasons not to choose it

Value proposition. A value proposition is the full set of benefits on which the brand is positioned. Kotler and Armstrong sum up the winning ones in five phrases.

Bases of positioning. A brand can be positioned on:

  • attributes (a phone's battery life) or benefits (all-day use without charging);
  • use or application (a cough syrup for night-time) or user (a shampoo for children);
  • competitor (better than the leader on one point) or product class (a juice against soft drinks);
  • price and quality.

An example. Imagine a new breakfast mix. Its positioning statement: “For working parents in cities, the breakfast mix ready in five minutes, because it needs only hot water.” The target is working parents and the category is breakfast mix. Speed is the point of difference; hot water is the reason to believe. Taste and nutrition must be points of parity, or the speed will not matter.

Don't confuse positioning with differentiation. Differentiation makes the offer actually different. Positioning decides which difference to stress, and how buyers should see it. And a point of parity is not a weakness: it is the minimum a buyer expects.

Where it breaks. A position cannot be claimed by advertising alone; if the product does not deliver, buyers will not hold the idea. A position that is too narrow can also limit growth, and changing an established position is slow and costly.

For exams. Expect Ries and Trout's line, the POD and POP distinction, and the five winning value propositions.

Go deeper for practitioners

Positioning errors. Kotler names four. Underpositioning: buyers have only a vague idea of the brand. Overpositioning: buyers have too narrow an idea of it. Confused positioning: too many claims, or the position changes too often. Doubtful positioning: buyers find the claims hard to believe, given the product, price or maker.

A decision. The breakfast brand's research finds that buyers love the speed but suspect the mix is unhealthy. That doubt is a missing point of parity, not a reason to drop the point of difference. The better move is to give a reason to believe on nutrition, such as listing the ingredients plainly on the front of the pack, while keeping speed at the centre.

Links. Brand management (this unit) takes positioning into brand equity.

Positioning lives in the customer's mind, not in the product.

blocks.title: Differentiation and the brand bull's-eye
blocks.html:
A tiffin service in Bengaluru tells customers its food is ‘tasty and hygienic’. Every rival says the same. A difference that every competitor also claims gives no one a reason to choose.

In plain wordsDifferentiation is making your offer different from rivals' in ways that buyers care about.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: differentiation is the process of adding a set of meaningful and valued differences to distinguish the company's offering from competitors' offerings.

A firm positions its offer by differentiating it from competitors'. Kotler and Keller name five main bases.

BasisVariablesExample
ProductForm, features, performance, conformance, durability, reliability, repairability, style, designPhones that compete on design and performance
ServicesOrdering ease, delivery, installation, customer training, customer consulting, maintenance and repair, returnsPizza chains competing on delivery time; air-conditioner makers on installation
PersonnelCompetence, courtesy, credibility, reliability, responsiveness, communicationService firms depend heavily on their people
ChannelCoverage, expertise, performanceE-commerce and other delivery-dependent businesses
ImageSymbols (such as McDonald's golden arches), atmosphere, media, events and sponsorshipsBrands built on a recognisable identity

Is it a real point of difference? Keller's three tests: it must be

  • desirable to consumers: personally relevant to them;
  • deliverable by the company: it has the resources and commitment to create and keep the association profitably;
  • differentiating from competitors: seen as distinctive and superior.

Back to the tiffin service. ‘Tasty and hygienic’ is desirable but fails the third test, since every rival claims it. ‘Delivered by 12.30 on every working day, or the meal is free’ is desirable and differentiating. It is deliverable only if the kitchen and riders can keep the promise; otherwise it costs more than it earns.

Points of parity come in three kinds:

KindMeaningExample
Category POPsWhat consumers see as essential for a credible offer in the category: necessary but not sufficient for choice; they change with technology, law and trendsA travel agency must book flights and hotels, advise on packages and offer payment options
Correlational POPsNegative associations that arise from the brand's own positive ones, which the brand must answerA low-priced brand reassuring buyers on quality
Competitive POPsAssociations designed to negate a competitor's points of differenceA bank app matching a rival's instant-transfer feature, so that the rival's advantage no longer counts

The brand-positioning bull's-eye (Kotler and Keller) communicates the positioning to everyone in the organisation. At its centre are the brand mantra (the brand's essence in a few words) and the key points of parity and difference. Around them are the reasons to believe, facts that support those points. The outer ring holds the brand's values, personality or character and its executional properties and visual identity. Boxes beside it record the inputs (the target consumer and a key insight; the competitive need and rival brands) and the output: the ideal consumer takeaway.

Don't confuse a point of difference with any difference. A difference counts only if it passes all three tests. Some study notes list only two kinds of points of parity, category and competitive; Kotler and Keller add a third, correlational, for the weakness a brand's own strengths create.

Where it breaks. Most product and service differences can be copied, so a point of difference wears out unless the firm renews it. Personnel differentiation depends on every employee, every day, which is hard to keep consistent across many branches.

For exams. Expect the five bases of differentiation, the three tests (desirable, deliverable, differentiating), the kinds of points of parity, and what sits at the centre of the bull's-eye.

Differentiate on product, services, people, channel or image; test it as desirable, deliverable, differentiating.

text: Segmentation starts from the fact that different audiences need different offers. The Kuṟaḷ asks speakers who are pure and know the range of words to study the assembly before they speak. It is about addressing a gathering, not about dividing a market.

chapters.title: Product Decisions: Levels, New Products and the Life Cycle
chapters.scope: What a product is to a buyer, how new products are developed and adopted, and how strategy changes as a product ages.

blocks.title: Product levels and classification
blocks.html:
Two phones have almost the same chip, camera and price. Buyers still pick one because its service centre is in their town, or because it comes with free backup. What people buy is more than the object in the box.

In plain wordsA product is whatever a buyer gets to meet a need, and it comes in layers: the benefit, the thing itself, and the extras around it.

Exam definitionA product is anything that can be offered to a market for attention, acquisition, use or consumption that might satisfy a want or need (Kotler and Armstrong).

Products include physical goods, services, experiences, events, places and ideas. Buyers see a product at several levels, and each level adds customer value.

LevelMeaningExample: a smartphone
Core product (core customer value)The basic benefit or problem-solving service the buyer is really seekingStaying connected
Actual productThe tangible offer: features, quality, design, brand name and packagingThe phone itself, its brand and box
Augmented productExtra services and benefits: delivery, installation, warranty, after-sales service, supportWarranty, repair network, cloud backup

Five levels. Kotler and Keller describe a five-level customer-value hierarchy. Take a guest at a hotel:

  1. Core benefit: rest and sleep.
  2. Basic product: a room with a bed, bathroom and towels.
  3. Expected product: what guests normally expect, such as clean sheets and a quiet room.
  4. Augmented product: more than they expect, such as an airport pickup.
  5. Potential product: all the changes the offer might undergo in future.

Competition increasingly takes place at the augmented level. Some texts call the actual product the formal product.

Classifying consumer products. Products are grouped by how people buy them. A kirana store lives on convenience products; a family visits three showrooms before buying a refrigerator, a shopping product.

TypeBuying behaviourExamples
ConvenienceBought often, quickly, with little comparisonSoap, newspapers, snacks
ShoppingCompared on quality, price and style before buyingFurniture, clothing, appliances
SpecialtyUnique features or brand; buyers make a special effortLuxury watches, designer clothes
UnsoughtNot known of, or not normally thought of buyingLife insurance, blood donation

Don't confuse the core product with the actual product. The core is the benefit, staying connected. The actual product is the thing that delivers it: the phone, its brand and its box. Also keep the two models apart: Kotler and Armstrong use three levels, Kotler and Keller five.

Where it breaks. The classes describe buyers, not goods. A watch is a shopping product for one buyer and a specialty product for another. In services, the actual and augmented levels often blur.

In practice. When rivals' actual products look alike, compete on the augmented level: delivery, installation, warranty and service. For exams, expect a level matched to an example, or the five levels in order.

Core benefit, actual product, augmented product.

blocks.title: Product mix and product lines
blocks.html:
A consumer-goods firm wants to grow. It can enter a new category, add brands to a category it already sells in, or add sizes and flavours to a brand. Each move stretches a different dimension of its product mix.

In plain wordsThe product mix is everything a firm sells, grouped into lines of related products.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the product mix, or product assortment, is the set of all product lines and items a particular seller offers for sale.

A product item is a specific version of a product: one model, brand or size. A product line is a group of closely related products made or sold by the same firm.

DimensionMeaningExample
WidthThe number of different product linesA consumer-goods firm with lines in personal wash, laundry, skin care, hair care, oral care, deodorants, tea and coffee has a width of eight
LengthThe total number of items across all its linesThose eight lines might hold 23 brands in all
DepthThe number of variants of each product in a line, by size, flavour, formulation and so onA toothpaste offered in three formulations and three sizes has a depth of 3 × 3 = 9
ConsistencyHow closely the lines are related in use, production, distribution or other waysLines all sold through grocery stores are consistent in distribution

Working it out. For the food company in the diagram, width is 3 and length is 7. Its average line length is length ÷ width = 7 ÷ 3 ≈ 2.3 brands per line. If biscuit brand 1 comes in two flavours and three pack sizes, its depth is 2 × 3 = 6.

These four dimensions give the firm four ways to grow: add lines (width), lengthen lines, add variants (depth), or make the mix more or less consistent.

Don't confuse length with depth. Length counts items across all lines. Depth counts the variants of one product inside a line. Nor is a product line the product mix: the mix is all the lines together.

Where it breaks. The counts depend on what the firm calls an item: a brand, a variant or each pack size. Compare two firms only on the same basis. A long line also costs more to stock and can confuse buyers.

In practice. A line is too short if adding items would raise profit, and too long if dropping items would (Kotler and Armstrong). Firms lengthen a line by stretching it up-market or down-market, or by filling gaps within its present range.

Width: lines. Length: items. Depth: variants. Consistency: relatedness.

blocks.title: New product development and adoption
blocks.html:
A dairy cooperative's staff suggest 25 new products in a year. Launching each one would cost crores, and most would not sell. The firm needs a sequence that drops weak ideas while they are still cheap to drop.

In plain wordsNew product development is the step-by-step path from an idea to a product on the shelf.

Exam definitionNew product development is the development of original products, product improvements, product modifications and new brands through the firm's own product development efforts (Kotler and Armstrong).

Kotler and Armstrong describe NPD in eight steps. Follow the dairy's idea for a packaged masala chaas, a spiced buttermilk, as an illustration.

StepWhat happensThe masala chaas
1 Idea generationSystematic search for ideas from customers, employees, competitors, suppliers and R&DField staff hear that buyers want a ready summer drink
2 Idea screeningDropping poor ideas early, since costs rise at each later step20 of the 25 ideas are dropped
3 Concept development and testingTurning the idea into a detailed concept and testing it with target customers200 households react to a description and a picture
4 Marketing strategy developmentPlanning the target market, positioning, price, distribution and marketing budgetTarget: office-goers; sold chilled through dairy booths
5 Business analysisEstimating sales, costs and profits to see if they meet the firm's objectivesWill it earn back its launch cost in two summers?
6 Product developmentBuilding a working prototype and testing itRecipe and pack tested for taste and shelf life
7 Test marketingTrying the product and its marketing in realistic market settingsOn sale in two cities for one season
8 CommercialisationFull launch: deciding when, where, to whom and howState-wide launch before the next summer

Adoption. After launch, buyers do not all arrive at once. Everett Rogers (Diffusion of Innovations, 1962) grouped adopters by how early they take up an innovation.

So of every 1,000 eventual buyers of the chaas, about 25 would be innovators and 135 early adopters. Another 340 would be the early majority, 340 the late majority and 160 laggards.

Don't confuse concept testing with test marketing. A concept test shows customers a description before the product exists. A test market sells the real product, with its real marketing, in a few places. Also, many study notes list seven steps and leave out step 4, marketing strategy development; Kotler and Armstrong give eight.

Where it breaks. In practice the steps overlap, and fast-moving firms run several at once. Test marketing costs time and money and lets competitors see the product early. Rogers's shares come from a normal curve, so a real product's adopters rarely split exactly that way.

For exams. Know the eight steps in order, the step short lists drop, and Rogers's five groups with their shares.

Go deeper for practitioners

What speeds adoption. Kotler and Keller list five traits of an innovation that affect how fast it spreads:

  • Relative advantage over what it replaces.
  • Compatibility with buyers' values and habits.
  • Complexity, which slows adoption.
  • Divisibility: whether it can be tried in small amounts.
  • Communicability: whether its benefits can be seen or described.

The chasm. Geoffrey Moore (Crossing the Chasm, 1991) argued that many technology products stall between early adopters and the early majority. The two groups buy for different reasons: the first for novelty, the second for proven, practical value.

A decision. Your concept test is strong, but a test market would take a full summer and show rivals your recipe. Skipping it saves a season but risks a state-wide flop. The cost of a failed full launch, against the cost of a lost season, decides it.

Links. The product life cycle (next) picks up where commercialisation ends: innovators buy in the introduction stage, the majorities in growth and maturity.

Generate, screen, test the concept, plan the strategy, analyse, develop, test-market, launch.

blocks.title: The product life cycle
blocks.html:
A new snack sells only through heavy advertising in its first year. Ten years later it sells by habit, while rivals undercut its price. The same product needs different marketing as it ages.

In plain wordsThe product life cycle is the usual path of a product's sales and profits, from launch to withdrawal.

Exam definitionThe product life cycle (PLC) is the course of a product's sales and profits over its lifetime (Kotler and Armstrong).

Each stage calls for a different strategy. Theodore Levitt's “Exploit the Product Life Cycle” (1965) is a classic account. Before the cycle starts, the product is in development: sales are zero and the firm is only spending.

AspectIntroductionGrowthMaturityDecline
SalesLowRising fastPeakFalling
ProfitsNegative or lowRisingHighDeclining
CustomersInnovatorsEarly adoptersMiddle majorityLaggards
CompetitorsFewGrowingStable, then decliningDeclining
Marketing objectiveCreate awareness and trialMaximise market shareMaximise profit while defending shareCut spending and milk the brand
ProductBasic productExtensions, service, warrantyDiversify brands and modelsPhase out weak items
PriceCost-plus, or skimmingPrice to penetrateMatch or beat competitorsCut price
DistributionSelectiveIntensiveMore intensiveSelective: drop unprofitable outlets
PromotionBuild awareness among early adopters and dealersBuild awareness and interest in the mass marketStress brand differences and benefitsReduce to the minimum needed to keep loyal customers

Reading the table down one column. In maturity, sales are at their peak but growing slowly, and many rivals compete for the same buyers. So the snack maker adds new flavours and pack sizes, matches rivals' prices, pushes into more outlets, and advertises what makes its brand different.

Not every product follows the smooth curve. Styles come and go in cycles, fashions rise slowly and decline slowly, and fads rise and collapse quickly.

Don't confuse a product class, a product form and a brand. The PLC can describe any of them, but they age differently. A class, such as packaged snacks, can stay mature for decades; a form, such as baked chips, or a single brand moves through the stages faster. Nor is a fashion a fad: a fashion declines slowly, a fad collapses.

Where it breaks. It is hard to tell which stage a product is in, or when the next one starts. The PLC can also fulfil itself: a manager who decides a product is declining cuts its support, and sales then fall. Many products are revived rather than left to decline.

In practice. Use the stage to set the objective, then check every element of the mix against it. For exams, expect a stage matched to a strategy row, and the difference between styles, fashions and fads.

Go deeper for practitioners

Three ways out of maturity. Kotler and Armstrong suggest modifying the market (new users, new uses, more use per buyer), modifying the product (quality, features, style) or modifying the marketing mix (price, channels, promotion).

The critique. Nariman Dhalla and Sonia Yuspeh's “Forget the Product Life Cycle Concept!” (1976) argued that the stages are not fixed and that the PLC can lead managers to drop products too early. Treat the curve as a description of the past, not a forecast.

A decision. A ten-year-old snack's sales fell 5% this year. Is it declining, or did a rival's discount take share for a season? Check whether the whole category fell or only your brand. A falling category points to decline; a falling brand in a steady category points to a fixable problem.

Links. Skimming and penetration are explained in Pricing decisions; intensive and selective distribution in Place: distribution channels, logistics and supply chains.

Introduce, grow, mature, decline: change the mix at each stage.

pairings.modern: The rise and fall of demand
text: The PLC describes sales that gather, peak and fall away. The Kuṟaḷ compares great wealth to a theatre crowd: it gathers like the audience for a show, and leaves as the crowd disperses when the show ends. The couplet is about the impermanence of riches, not about products.

chapters.title: Brand Management: Equity, Strategy and Loyalty
chapters.scope: What a brand is worth, the decisions that build it, how brands are extended, and how loyal their buyers become.

blocks.title: Brands and brand equity
blocks.html:
Two 10 kg packs of atta sit side by side in a kirana store. One carries a well-known name and costs more; the other has no name. Many shoppers still pick the named pack, and that extra pull is what brand equity measures.

In plain wordsA brand is the name and signs that tell buyers who made a product. Brand equity is the extra value that name adds in buyers' minds.

Exam definitionA brand is a name, term, sign, symbol or design, or a combination of them, intended to identify the goods or services of one seller or group of sellers and to differentiate them from those of competitors (American Marketing Association).

A brand strategy is the long-term plan to build, position and sustain the brand. Unlike a campaign, it is long-term and emotion-driven. It aims at growth, customer loyalty and a strong market position.

What brands do.

  • For consumers: a brand identifies the maker, so buyers can hold it responsible. The same product can be judged differently depending on how it is branded. Brands simplify decisions and reduce risk.
  • For firms: brands simplify handling and record-keeping, and give legal protection (trademarks for names, patents for processes, copyright and designs for packaging). They signal quality, so satisfied buyers can choose again. Loyalty makes demand predictable and builds barriers to entry. Kotler and Keller note that loyalty can let a brand charge 20 to 25 per cent more than competitors.

Rivals can copy processes and designs, but not the impressions that years of experience and marketing leave in buyers' minds.

An illustration. Suppose the named atta sells for ₹480 and the unnamed pack of the same flour for ₹430. If the brand sells 1 lakh packs a month, the ₹50 premium is worth ₹50 lakh a month (₹50 × 1,00,000). That premium is one visible sign of brand equity.

AspectBrand equityBrand value
MeaningThe added value a brand gives a product in customers' mindsThe brand's financial worth
NatureTrust, preference and loyaltyA monetary asset
Shows inCustomers paying a premium, as for AppleValuations in mergers and acquisitions

Keller's definition. Kevin Lane Keller defines customer-based brand equity as the differential effect that brand knowledge has on consumer response to the marketing of that brand. It has three ingredients:

  1. Equity arises from differences in consumer response. If customers respond no differently to a branded product than to an unbranded one, the product is essentially a commodity, and competition will probably be based on price.
  2. Those differences come from consumers' brand knowledge: all the thoughts, feelings, images, experiences and beliefs linked to the brand. These must be strong, favourable and unique, as Toyota's link to reliability is.
  3. Equity shows in perceptions, preferences and behaviour across all of the brand's marketing.

Equity is positive when consumers react more favourably to the marketing once they know the brand, and negative when they react less favourably. The brand promise is the marketer's vision of what the brand must be and do for consumers.

ModelComponents
David Aaker (1991)Brand loyalty, brand awareness, perceived quality, brand associations, and other proprietary assets such as patents
Keller's customer-based brand equity pyramidSalience (identity), then performance and imagery (meaning), then judgements and feelings (response), and at the top resonance (relationship)

Don't confuse brand equity with brand value. Equity lives in customers' minds and shows in how they respond. Value is a money figure put on the brand, for example when a firm is bought. Strong equity usually raises value, but the two are measured differently.

Where it breaks. Equity is hard to measure directly. Surveys record what people say, and a price premium can also come from wider distribution or habit. Equity can turn negative too: after a scandal, buyers may respond worse to the brand than to no brand at all.

For exams. Expect the AMA definition of a brand, Keller's definition of customer-based brand equity and its three ingredients, and the difference between equity and value.

Equity lives in customers' minds; value is what the brand is worth in money.

blocks.title: Brand equity models
blocks.html:
A brand that every household knows can still be losing buyers. Brand equity models split a brand's strength into parts, so a manager can see which part is weak.

In plain wordsA brand equity model is a framework that breaks a brand's strength into parts that can be measured and managed.

Exam definitionBrand equity is a set of brand assets and liabilities linked to a brand, its name and symbol, that add to or subtract from the value provided by a product or service to a firm and/or to that firm's customers (David Aaker, 1991).

Kotler and Keller describe several models of brand equity. They share principles but stress different things.

1. Young and Rubicam's BrandAsset Valuator (BAV) rests on four pillars.

PillarMeasures
Energised differentiationHow far the brand is seen as different from others, and its momentum and leadership
RelevanceHow appropriate and broad the brand's appeal is
EsteemHow well the brand is regarded and respected: perceived quality and loyalty
KnowledgeHow aware and familiar consumers are with the brand
  • Brand strength = differentiation + relevance. It is a leading indicator of future growth.
  • Brand stature = esteem + knowledge. It is a report card on past performance.

Plotting strength against stature gives a power grid of the brand's stage of development. New brands show more differentiation and energy than relevance, with low esteem and knowledge. Leadership brands are high on all four. Declining brands show high knowledge but lower esteem, and lower still relevance and differentiation.

An illustration. Imagine a hair-oil brand that every family in a town knows, but young buyers find old-fashioned. It scores high on knowledge and low on relevance and differentiation: the pattern of a declining brand. Being famous is not the same as being strong.

2. Millward Brown's BrandZ places consumers on a brand dynamics pyramid.

LevelThe consumer…
PresenceIs actively familiar with the brand, through trial, salience or knowledge of its promise
RelevanceFinds it relevant to their needs, in the right price range or in the consideration set
PerformanceBelieves it performs acceptably and puts it on the short-list
AdvantageBelieves it has an emotional or rational advantage over others in the category
BondingIs attached to it, rationally and emotionally, to the exclusion of most other brands

Bonded consumers build stronger relationships with the brand and spend more on it. Most consumers sit at the lower levels, so the marketer's task is to move them up.

3. Keller's brand resonance model sees brand building as four ascending steps, each answering a consumer's question. The steps rest on six building blocks. Resonance, at the top, is the intensity of the customer's bond with the brand, seen in brands such as Harley-Davidson and Apple.

The left side of the pyramid is the rational route and the right side the emotional route. MasterCard combined both, stressing worldwide acceptance and, in its ‘Priceless’ campaign, the things money can't buy.

4. Aaker's model (1991) groups the assets and liabilities in his definition under five heads: brand loyalty, brand awareness, perceived quality, brand associations, and other proprietary assets such as patents and trademarks.

Don't confuse brand strength with brand stature. Strength (differentiation and relevance) looks forward; stature (esteem and knowledge) looks back. Keep the two pyramids apart too: BrandZ has five levels, from presence to bonding; Keller's has four steps on six blocks, from salience to resonance.

Where it breaks. Each model organises survey measures; none is a law. They name different parts, so a brand's equity looks different depending on the model used. BAV and BrandZ come from commercial research firms and rest on their own survey data.

For exams. Expect a model matched to its parts, the order of the BrandZ and Keller pyramids, and which BAV pillars make up strength and stature.

BAV's four pillars, BrandZ's pyramid, Keller's resonance, Aaker's five assets.

blocks.title: Major brand strategy decisions
blocks.html:
A spice maker in Pune is about to launch a range of masalas. Before the first pack is printed, it must decide what the brand stands for, what to call it, whose name goes on it, and how the brand will grow.

In plain wordsBrand strategy decisions are the choices a firm makes about how a brand is positioned, named, owned and grown.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a firm's branding strategy, often called its brand architecture, is the number and nature of the common and distinctive brand elements it applies to the products it sells.

Kotler and Armstrong group the choices into four decisions.

DecisionOptions
Brand positioningOn product attributes, on benefits, or, the strongest, on beliefs and values that carry emotional weight
Brand name selectionA good name suggests the benefits, is easy to say and remember, distinctive, extendable, translatable, legally protectable, and free of bad meanings in other languages
Brand sponsorshipManufacturer's (national) brand, private (store) brand, licensed brand, or co-branding
Brand developmentLine extensions, brand extensions, multibrands or new brands

Three levels of positioning, for the masala brand. On an attribute: ‘no added colour’. On a benefit: ‘tastes like spices ground at home’. On beliefs and values: ‘cook for your family the way your mother did’. Positioning on attributes is the least effective level, since attributes are easy to copy. Benefits link the name with something desirable; beliefs and values tap emotions.

Sponsorship decides whose name the product carries. It can be the maker's own, a retailer's (a supermarket's own-label masala), a name licensed from another owner, or two brands together. Licensing leases a brand name for use in a defined way, territory and period.

StrategyHow it works
Individual namesA separate name for each product; one failure does not harm the company name
Blanket family nameOne name for all products; new products gain acceptance quickly
Separate family namesA different family name for each category
Corporate name with individual namesThe company name legitimises the product, the individual name gives it its own identity

To brand a new product, a firm can develop new brand elements, apply some of its existing ones, or combine new and existing elements.

TermMeaning
Brand lineAll products sold under one brand
Brand mix (assortment)All the brand lines a seller offers
Branded variantsVersions of a brand made for particular retailers or channels, for example a slightly different model of a mattress for each large chain
Licensed productA product carrying a brand that its owner has licensed to another manufacturer

Don't confuse brand sponsorship with sponsoring an event. Here sponsorship means whose brand name the product carries. Keep brand line and brand mix apart too: a line is all products under one brand; the mix is all the lines a seller offers.

Where it breaks. Positioning on beliefs and values is strongest only when the product delivers and the values fit the buyers; otherwise it reads as an empty claim. A blanket family name cuts launch costs but shares risk: one product's failure can harm every product under the name.

For exams. Expect the four decisions in order, the naming strategies matched to their effect, and the three levels of positioning.

Position, name, sponsor, develop.

blocks.title: Brand portfolios
blocks.html:
A detergent maker sells one premium brand. A rival launches a cheap powder and starts taking buyers. Cutting the premium brand's price would hurt its image and its margin, so the firm needs another answer.

In plain wordsA brand portfolio is the full set of brands a firm sells in one market, where each brand has a job to do.

Exam definitionThe brand portfolio is the set of all brands and brand lines a particular firm offers for sale in a particular category or market segment (Kotler and Keller).

A brand can be stretched only so far, and not every segment the firm wants will view one brand equally well. So firms often need several brands.

Why have several brands in one category?

  • to gain more shelf space and make retailers depend more on the firm;
  • to keep variety-seeking consumers who would otherwise switch to a rival;
  • to create internal competition;
  • to gain economies of scale in advertising, selling, merchandising and distribution.
RoleWhat it doesExample
Flanker (fighter)Positioned against competitors' brands so that the more important, more profitable flagship can keep its desired positionA cheaper second brand launched against a price-cutting rival
Cash cowKept despite falling sales because it stays profitable with almost no marketing support; the firm ‘milks’ its reservoir of equityAn older car model kept on sale because withdrawing it might not move buyers to the firm's other models
Low-end entry levelA relatively low-priced ‘traffic builder’ that draws customers into the brand franchise so they can later be traded upEntry models of a luxury carmaker
High-end prestigeA relatively high-priced brand that adds prestige and credibility to the whole portfolioA flagship superbike that draws visitors to the showroom and lifts the image of the maker's other motorcycles

Back to the detergent. As an illustration, the premium brand sells at ₹200 a kilo and the rival at ₹110. The firm launches a flanker at ₹120 a kilo under a new name. The flanker fights on price, and the premium brand keeps its position and its margin.

Sizing the portfolio. If dropping a brand would raise total profit, the portfolio is too big. If adding one would raise it, the portfolio is too small.

Don't confuse a flanker with an entry-level brand. Both may be cheap. A flanker exists to fight a rival and protect the flagship; an entry brand exists to bring new buyers in and trade them up later. A cash-cow brand is also not the BCG matrix's cash cow, which is a business with a high share of a slow-growing market.

Where it breaks. Every extra brand needs its own marketing money. Brands placed too close together take sales from each other rather than from rivals. A flanker that is too good can pull buyers down from the flagship.

For exams. Expect a description matched to one of the four roles, and the reasons for keeping several brands in one category.

Flankers, cash cows, entry brands, prestige brands.

blocks.title: Brand extensions
blocks.html:
A noodle brand that every household knows wants to sell ketchup. Using its famous name could save years of advertising. It could also blur what the name stands for.

In plain wordsA brand extension uses a name buyers already know to launch a new product.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a brand extension is a firm's use of an established brand to introduce a new product.

The established brand is the parent brand. A parent brand that supports several extensions is a family or master brand. A sub-brand combines a new name with an existing one, as in Cadbury Dairy Milk Silk.

TypeWhat changesExample
Line extensionA new item in the same category under the same brand: new flavours, forms, sizes or packagingA new noodle variety under a noodle brand
Category extensionThe brand enters a different product categoryA noodle brand launching ketchup

Kotler and Armstrong's four brand development choices form a grid.

Multibrands are new brands in an existing category, used to capture different segments. A flanker or fighter brand, a lower-priced brand launched to protect the flagship, is one use of them.

An illustration of the cost argument. Suppose building awareness for a new ketchup brand would need ₹40 crore of advertising. Under the noodle name, the campaign need only introduce the product, so ₹15 crore might do. The ₹25 crore difference is the saving from extending.

AdvantagesLimitations
Lower perceived risk for buyers; quicker acceptanceBrand dilution: the brand's meaning blurs
Lower marketing and launch costsConsumer confusion
Can strengthen the parent brandRetailer resistance to more variants
Wider market coverageCannibalisation of the parent's sales; a failure can hurt the parent; a missed chance to build a new brand

Co-branding puts two established brands on one product, so each brand's strength supports the other.

Don't confuse the two uses of ‘brand extension’. In Kotler and Keller, brand extension is the umbrella term, covering both line and category extensions. In Kotler and Armstrong's grid, a brand extension means a new category only, and a line extension is a separate choice. Check which usage a question follows.

Where it breaks. The brand may become less strongly tied to any one product. A brand known for Ayurvedic products that moves into jeans, for example, risks its specific meaning. Inappropriate extensions can confuse buyers and make them question the brand's integrity.

In practice. Before extending, ask two questions. Do the parent's associations fit the new category? And will the new product add to what the brand means, or blur it?

Go deeper for practitioners

Why extensions succeed more often. Consumers form expectations from what they know of the parent. Retailers are readier to stock the product. The launch campaign need only introduce the product, not the brand too. The firm saves the cost of a new name and gains packaging and labelling efficiencies. Extensions can also feed back positively: they can clarify the brand's meaning, renew interest in it, widen its coverage and open the way to further extensions.

How much damage a failure does. The worst case, an extension that fails and harms the parent, is rare. ‘Marketing failures’, where too few people try the product, do much less damage than ‘product failures’, where it fails to live up to its promise. Even product failures dilute equity mainly when the extension closely resembles the parent.

A decision. As an illustration, the noodle brand's ketchup sells 10 lakh bottles a month. Research shows 4 lakh of those buyers used to buy the firm's own older sauce. That looks like cannibalisation: 40% of the new sales came from the firm itself. But if those buyers were about to switch to a rival's ketchup, the loss is pre-emptive cannibalisation, and the firm is better off taking its own sales than losing them.

Extend the line, extend the brand, add brands, or start anew.

blocks.title: Brand loyalty
blocks.html:
Two regulars buy tea at the same stall near a bus stand. One walks past a cheaper stall every day to get there; the other moves whenever a rival offers ₹2 off. Both buy often, but only one is loyal.

In plain wordsBrand loyalty is how firmly a customer sticks to a brand: buying it again and speaking well of it, whatever rivals do to tempt them away.

Exam definitionA standard definition, after Richard Oliver (1999): loyalty is a deeply held commitment to rebuy or repatronise a preferred product or service consistently in the future, despite situational influences and marketing efforts that could cause switching.

Loyalty shows in repeat purchases and in positive behaviour such as word-of-mouth advocacy. David Aaker (1991) arranged its levels in a pyramid, from no loyalty at the base to full commitment at the top.

LevelBuyer
1 SwitchersPrice-sensitive and indifferent; no loyalty to any brand
2 Habitual buyersSatisfied or at least not dissatisfied; no reason to change
3 Satisfied buyers with switching costsWould lose time, money or risk by changing
4 Brand likersLike the brand and regard it as a friend
5 Committed buyersProud to use the brand and recommend it

Back to the tea stall. The customer who moves for ₹2 off is a switcher. A customer who comes only because the stall is on the way is a habitual buyer. One who would lose the free tenth cup on a loyalty card by going elsewhere has a switching cost. The one who walks past the cheaper stall, and brings friends, is a brand liker or a committed buyer.

Don't confuse repeat buying with loyalty. A habitual buyer repeats out of convenience and leaves when a rival makes switching easy; a committed buyer stays and recommends. Study notes often give the levels in a muddled order; the version here follows Aaker.

Where it breaks. The pyramid sorts buyers; it does not measure them. One person can be committed to a brand of tea and a switcher on detergent. Loyalty programmes can raise switching costs (level 3) without making anyone like the brand.

For exams. Expect the five levels in order from base to top, and a description matched to its level.

Switchers, habitual, switching costs, likers, committed.

text: Brand equity is reputation that has become an asset. The Kuṟaḷ says that to give and to live with renown is the only real gain of life. It speaks of a person's good name earned through generosity, not of a commercial brand.
pairings.quote: “To give, and to live with renown: there is no other gain for a life.” ஈதல் இசைபட வாழ்தல் அதுவல்லது ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 231

text: Co-branding lends one brand the standing of another. The Kuṟaḷ says that goodness of mind brings prosperity, and good company brings every kind of renown. It is about a person's associates, not about brand partnerships.
pairings.quote: “Goodness of mind brings prosperity to people; goodness of company brings all renown.” மனநலம் மன்னுயிர்க் காக்கம் இனநலம் எல்லாப் புகழும் தரும். Tirukkuṟaḷ 457

text: A weak extension is seen at once because the parent is so well known. The Kuṟaḷ says a fault in those of noble family stands out like the spot on the moon high in the sky. Its subject is conduct and lineage, not brands.
pairings.quote: “A fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon high in the sky.” குடிப்பிறந்தார் கண்விளங்கும் குற்றம் விசும்பின் மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து. Tirukkuṟaḷ 957

text: At the top of Aaker's pyramid, committed buyers forgive a lapse. The Kuṟaḷ says those whose friendship has grown out of love do not withdraw their love even when the friend does them harm. It describes friendship, not a customer's tie to a brand.
pairings.quote: “Those whose friendship grew from love do not give up that love even when the friend brings them ruin.” அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார் அன்பின் வழிவந்த கேண்மை யவர். Tirukkuṟaḷ 807

chapters.title: Pricing Decisions: Objectives, Factors and Strategies
chapters.scope: Why firms price as they do, what limits them, and the main pricing strategies.

blocks.title: Pricing objectives and factors
blocks.html:
A home baker in Pune has a new cake that costs her ₹300 to make. Rival bakeries charge ₹450 to ₹550 for similar cakes, and her regulars would pay up to ₹700. What she wants from the cake decides where in that range she prices it.

In plain wordsPrice is what a buyer gives up to get a product: mostly money, but also time and effort.

Exam definitionPrice is the amount of money charged for a product or service. More broadly, it is the sum of all the values that customers give up to gain the benefits of having or using a product or service (Kotler and Armstrong).

Price is the only element of the marketing mix that produces revenue; the others are costs. It is also the most flexible, since it can be changed quickly.

Who sets prices. In small firms, the owner. In large ones, division and product-line managers, within policies set by top management. Where pricing is critical, as in aerospace, railways and oil, firms often have a pricing department.

Pricing objectives. The objective is what the firm wants price to achieve. The last column shows where the baker might price under each one.

ObjectiveWhat the firm doesThe baker's cake (illustrative)
SurvivalPrices just to cover variable costs and some fixed costs, to stay in business through overcapacity, intense competition or changing wantsNear ₹300, or briefly below it, so long as ingredients are covered
Maximum current profitSets the price that gives the highest short-run profitWherever her estimates of demand and cost show the highest profit
Maximum market share (penetration)Sets a low price to attract buyers quickly and gain share, expecting lower unit costs with volumeAbout ₹450, the bottom of the rivals' range
Maximum market skimmingSets a high initial price for early adopters, then lowers it over timeNear ₹700 at launch, lower once the novelty fades
Product-quality leadershipPrices high to signal and pay for superior qualityNear ₹700, backed by better ingredients

Other objectives include pricing low to discourage new entrants, pricing to keep the loyalty and support of channel members, pricing for a sales promotion, and pricing one product to help the sales of others.

InternalExternal
Costs (the floor for price)Customers' perceived value and demand, including price elasticity (the ceiling)
Overall marketing objectives and positioningCompetitors' prices and offers
The rest of the marketing mixThe economy: inflation, recession, interest rates
Brand imageGovernment regulation and channel members' reactions

Don't confuse a pricing objective with a pricing method. The objective is what the firm wants from price, such as market share. The method is how it calculates the figure, such as a mark-up on cost. One method can serve several objectives.

Where it breaks. The floor and ceiling are not fixed lines. A firm may price below full cost for a while, and each customer puts the ceiling at a different height. Maximum current profit needs demand and cost estimates that firms rarely have.

Costs set the floor, customer value the ceiling, competitors the range between.

blocks.title: Setting the price
blocks.html:
A shopper sees a pressure cooker at ₹299 and wonders what is wrong with it; at ₹9,999 she walks past. The same buyer has a price below which she distrusts the quality, and one above which nothing seems worth it.

In plain wordsBuyers do not take a price at face value; they compare it with prices they already have in mind.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: reference prices are prices that buyers carry in their minds and refer to when they look at a given product.

Consumer psychology. Economists traditionally treated consumers as ‘price takers’. Marketers know that buyers interpret prices in the light of past purchases, advertising, friends and family, and the point of sale. Decisions rest on how consumers perceive prices. Buyers may have a lower threshold, below which a price signals poor quality, and an upper threshold, above which the product seems not worth the money.

StepWhat it involves
1 Select the pricing objectiveSurvival, maximum current profit, maximum market share, maximum market skimming or product-quality leadership
2 Determine demandDifferent prices lead to different demand, depending on the market (pure competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, pure monopoly) and on price elasticity. Demand sets the ceiling.
3 Estimate costsFixed, variable, total and average costs set the floor. In target costing the firm starts from the price the market will pay and designs the product to meet the cost that allows
4 Analyse competitors' costs, prices and offersThe three Cs: the company's costs (the floor), competitors' prices (an orienting point), and customers' perceived value (the ceiling)
5 Select a pricing methodCost-based: mark-up (cost-plus), target-return (return on investment), break-even, marginal-cost or full-cost (absorption) pricing. Value-based: perceived-value pricing, or value pricing (high quality at a fairly low price). Competition-based: going-rate or sealed-bid (auction) pricing
6 Select the final priceConsidering psychological pricing, the influence of the other mix elements, company pricing policies, and the effect on distributors, the sales force, competitors and government

Two cost-based methods, worked. Take an illustrative mixer-grinder maker in Pune. Its variable cost is ₹1,000 a unit, fixed costs are ₹30 lakh a year, and it expects to sell 10,000 units.

Unit cost = variable cost + fixed cost ÷ unit sales = ₹1,000 + ₹30,00,000 ÷ 10,000 = ₹1,300

Mark-up pricing. The firm wants a mark-up of 20% on the selling price:

Mark-up price = unit cost ÷ (1 − desired return on sales) = ₹1,300 ÷ 0.80 = ₹1,625

Target-return pricing. The firm has invested ₹1 crore and wants a 20% return on it, that is ₹20 lakh a year:

Target-return price = unit cost + (desired return × invested capital) ÷ unit sales = ₹1,300 + ₹20,00,000 ÷ 10,000 = ₹1,500

Break-even. At ₹1,500, each unit leaves ₹500 over its variable cost, so the firm covers its fixed costs after ₹30,00,000 ÷ ₹500 = 6,000 units.

Don't confuse a mark-up on cost with a mark-up on price. 20% on the ₹1,300 cost gives ₹1,560; 20% of the selling price gives ₹1,625. Also keep target costing apart from cost-plus: cost-plus starts from cost and adds a margin, while target costing starts from the price and works back to the cost.

Where it breaks. Both formulas assume the firm sells the 10,000 units it expects; at 6,000 units and ₹1,500 it merely breaks even. Mark-up pricing ignores demand, perceived value and competition.

For exams. Know the six steps in order, the three Cs, and which methods are cost-, value- or competition-based.

Objective, demand, costs, competitors, method, final price.

blocks.title: Pricing strategies
blocks.html:
A firm launching a smart-watch can start at ₹15,000 and cut the price each year, or start at ₹6,000 and try to sign up buyers fast. Each route suits a different market.

In plain wordsA pricing strategy is a firm's standing rule for its price: built from cost, from value or from rivals, or a launch plan that changes over time.

Exam definitionMarket-skimming pricing sets a high price for a new product to skim maximum revenues layer by layer from the segments willing to pay it. Market-penetration pricing sets a low price for a new product to attract a large number of buyers and a large market share (Kotler and Armstrong).

StrategyHow it worksSuits
Cost-plus (mark-up)Adds a standard mark-up to costSimple; ignores demand and competition
Target-return (break-even)Sets the price that gives a target return on investmentUtilities and regulated firms
Value-based (perceived value)Sets price from buyers' perception of value, not from costDifferentiated products
Going-rate (competition-based)Prices at or near competitors' pricesCommodities and oligopolies
PremiumPrices deliberately above the nearest competitors to signal higher qualityBrands with a quality reputation
CustomaryKeeps a price buyers have come to expect, adjusting the product rather than the priceLow-priced snacks and confectionery
Everyday low pricing (EDLP)Keeps prices consistently low, with few temporary discountsDiscount retailers
Market skimmingHigh launch price, lowered over timeInnovative products, buyers willing to pay, few competitors able to enter quickly
Market penetrationLow launch price to win share fastPrice-sensitive markets where costs fall with volume and low prices deter competitors
PsychologicalUses price perceptions: odd prices such as ₹99 or ₹399, which buyers read as nearer the lower hundred; reference prices; price as a signal of qualityConsumer goods
Differential (discriminatory)Different prices to different customers, product forms, places or times, not reflecting cost differencesStudents' discounts, peak and off-peak fares
