BundleSeveral products together at a reduced priceCombos, packaged services

Don't confuse penetration with a launch offer. A common definition says penetration pricing means launching low and then raising the price. Penetration aims to win share with a low price; it does not require a later rise, and many penetration prices stay low. Nor is skimming the same as premium pricing: a premium price stays above rivals for good, while a skimming price is meant to come down.

Where it breaks. A skimming price shows rivals there is money to be made, and early buyers may resent the later cuts. A penetration price can start a price war, and buyers won only by price leave for a cheaper offer.

For exams. Expect the conditions for skimming and for penetration, and a strategy matched to an example.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. A Pune start-up launches a water purifier with a better filter. Its unit cost falls sharply only above about 50,000 units a year, and a larger rival could copy it within a year. Novelty argues for skimming; the cost curve and the threat of copying argue for penetration. A middle route: skim with a top model, and have a cheaper one ready before the rival arrives.

Links. Elasticity of demand (Unit 1) tells you whether a price cut will raise revenue, the test behind penetration. The product life cycle (Product decisions, this unit) places these launch choices in the introduction stage.

Skim when buyers pay for novelty; penetrate when volume lowers cost.

blocks.title: Adapting the price
blocks.html:
A pressure-cooker maker in Delhi sells one model to a dealer next door, a distributor in Kochi, a hotel chain buying 500 units, and a shopper at a Diwali sale. One list price cannot serve all four.

In plain wordsAdapting the price means changing what each buyer actually pays, by place, timing, quantity, type of buyer and promotion, starting from one list price.

Exam definitionPrice discrimination occurs when a company sells a product or service at two or more prices that do not reflect a proportional difference in costs (Kotler and Keller).

Firms build a price structure that reflects differences in geography, segment, timing, order size, delivery and service, so they seldom earn the same profit on every unit. Kotler and Keller name four kinds of adaptation.

1. Geographical pricing, including countertrade when buyers cannot pay in cash.

FormHow it works
Geographical pricingDeciding what to charge customers in different places: whether to charge distant buyers more for shipping, how to handle exchange rates, and how to be paid. Methods include point-of-production (FOB-origin) pricing, where each buyer pays freight from the factory; uniform delivered pricing, the same price plus freight for everyone; zone pricing, one price within each zone; and freight-absorption pricing, where the seller bears part of the freight to win business
BarterBuyer and seller exchange goods directly, with no money and no third party
Compensation dealThe seller takes part of the payment in cash and the rest in products
Buyback arrangementThe seller supplies a plant, equipment or technology and accepts part payment in products made with it
OffsetThe seller is paid in full in cash but agrees to spend a substantial amount in that country within a set time

2. Discounts and allowances. Take an illustrative bill of ₹1,00,000 to the Kochi distributor on terms of ‘2/10, net 30’. If it pays within 10 days, it deducts 2% and pays ₹98,000; otherwise the full ₹1,00,000 is due within 30 days.

KindGiven for
Cash discountPaying bills promptly
Quantity discountBuying large volumes
Functional (trade) discountChannel members who perform functions such as selling, storing and record-keeping
Seasonal discountBuying out of season
AllowanceExtra payment for resellers who join special programmes, such as trade-in or promotional allowances

3. Promotional pricing, to pull buyers in now.

TechniqueHow it works
Loss-leader pricingCutting the price of well-known brands to draw traffic into the store
Special-event pricingSpecial prices in certain seasons, such as year-end offers
Special-customer pricingPrices offered only to certain customers
Cash rebatesCash back for buying within a set period
Low-interest financing and longer payment termsCheap credit, or loans stretched to lower monthly payments, instead of a price cut
Warranties and service contractsAdding free or low-cost cover
Psychological discountingSetting an artificially high reference price and offering big ‘savings’ from it; it misleads buyers if the ‘was’ price was never really charged

4. Differentiated pricing, which is price discrimination in the sense defined above.

KindExample
Customer-segment pricingLower museum fees for students and senior citizens
Product-form pricingA large bottle of water priced lower per litre than a small one, not in proportion to cost
Image pricingThe same perfume sold at two prices in different bottles with different names and images
Channel pricingA soft drink costing more in a fine restaurant than from a vending machine
Location pricingDifferent prices for seats at a stadium, though each costs the same to provide
Time pricingPrices that vary by season, day or hour, such as peak and off-peak tariffs

Don't confuse price discrimination with prices that differ because costs differ. Charging more to deliver to a distant town covers real freight; charging students less for the same museum visit does not reflect cost. Only the second is price discrimination. Also keep a functional discount, paid for work the channel does, apart from a quantity discount, paid for volume.

Where it breaks. Buyers in the low-price group may resell to the high-price group. Frequent discounts teach buyers to wait for the sale.

For exams. Name the four kinds and the four forms of countertrade. An offset is paid fully in cash; a buyback partly in products made with the seller's equipment.

Go deeper for practitioners

When differentiated pricing works. Kotler and Keller set out its conditions. The market must divide into segments with different intensities of demand. Buyers in the lower-price segment must not be able to resell to the higher-price one. Competitors must not be able to undersell the firm in the higher-price segment. Segmenting and policing the market must cost less than the extra revenue. The practice must not breed customer resentment, and it must be legal.

Links. Market structures (Unit 1) covers Pigou's three degrees of price discrimination.

Geography, discounts, promotions, differentiation.

blocks.title: Price-quality strategies
blocks.html:
A new mixer-grinder brand must decide whether to sell a sturdy machine at a low price, an ordinary one at an ordinary price, or a fancy one at a high price. Shoppers who cannot test the motor will judge it partly by its price.

In plain wordsA firm chooses both how good its product is and what it charges, and buyers judge the pair together.

Exam definitionKotler's nine price-quality strategies combine three levels of product quality (high, medium, low) with three levels of price (high, medium, low).

When a firm enters a market or launches a product, it must decide where to place it on this price-quality map. Where buyers lack information about quality, they tend to take price as its signal.

Product qualityHigh priceMedium priceLow price
High1 Premium strategy2 High-value strategy3 Super-value strategy
Medium4 Overcharging strategy5 Medium-value strategy6 Good-value strategy
Low7 Rip-off strategy8 False-economy strategy9 Economy strategy

How the zones behave. The diagonal strategies (1, 5 and 9) can coexist in one market, so long as there are buyers who want each. A premium mixer at ₹8,000 and an economy one at ₹2,000 can both sell, to different shoppers. Strategies 2, 3 and 6 attack the diagonal by offering more quality for the price. Strategies 4, 7 and 8 overprice the product for its quality; customers feel cheated and complain, so they are hard to sustain.

Don't confuse the super-value strategy with the economy strategy. Both charge a low price. Economy gives low quality for it and sits on the diagonal; super-value gives high quality for it and attacks the brands above.

Where it breaks. Price works as a quality signal mainly when buyers cannot judge quality themselves; reviews and experience weaken it. An attacking strategy survives only if the firm's costs let it give more for less. And quality here means quality as buyers perceive it.

For exams. Expect a cell named from its price and quality, or the reverse. Remember the pattern: diagonal coexists, above it attacks, below it overprices.

Price should match quality; more quality for the price attacks, less quality for the price fails.

pairings.modern: Cost and market factors in price
text: Manu tells the king to fix the buying and selling rates of goods after weighing where they come from and where they go, how long they have been stored, and the gain and loss on them, and to review those rates publicly every five nights or every fortnight. These are the cost and market factors any price still has to reckon with, though the verse describes prices set by the ruler, not by firms.
pairings.quote: आगमं निर्गमं स्थानं तथा वृद्धिक्षयावुभौ । विचार्य सर्वपण्यानां कारयेत्क्रयविक्रयौ । āgamaṃ nirgamaṃ sthānaṃ tathā vṛddhikṣayāv ubhau / vicārya sarvapaṇyānāṃ kārayet krayavikrayau. “After weighing the arrival and dispatch, the storage, and the gain and loss of all goods, he should fix their buying and selling prices.” Manusmṛti 8.401; review at 8.402

chapters.title: Place: Distribution Channels, Logistics and Supply Chains
chapters.scope: How products reach customers: the channels they pass through, the logistics that move them, and the supply chain behind them.

blocks.title: Distribution channels
blocks.html:
A biscuit maker in Indore cannot open a shop in every town, and a kirana store cannot buy from fifty factories one by one. Firms in between solve this, and choosing them is among the hardest decisions a producer makes.

In plain wordsA distribution channel is the line of businesses a product passes through on its way from the maker to the buyer.

Exam definitionMarketing channels are sets of interdependent organisations participating in the process of making a product or service available for use or consumption (Kotler and Keller).

A channel transfers ownership from the point of production to the point of consumption. It is also called a marketing or trade channel. Channels form part of a wider value network: the partnerships and alliances a firm creates to source, augment and deliver its offerings.

Why intermediaries save effort. Take an illustration: 5 biscuit makers each selling to 100 kirana stores need 5 × 100 = 500 separate contacts. Through one distributor, they need 5 + 100 = 105.

KindRoleExamples
MerchantsBuy, take title to and resell the goodsWholesalers, retailers
AgentsSearch for customers and may negotiate for the producer, but do not take titleBrokers, manufacturers' representatives, sales agents
FacilitatorsAssist distribution but neither take title nor negotiateTransport firms, independent warehouses, banks, advertising agencies

Channel functions. Channel members gather information about customers and competitors, spread persuasive communications, and negotiate price and terms. They also place orders, finance inventories and bear the risks of channel work. Finally, they store and move products, arrange payment through banks, and oversee the transfer of ownership. Together these save the producer money, time and effort.

TypeHow it works
DirectThe producer sells straight to the final customer, without intermediaries
IndirectThe producer uses intermediaries such as wholesalers and retailers
Hybrid (multichannel)The producer combines direct and indirect channels for reach and convenience
LevelPath
Zero-level (direct)Producer → consumer
One-levelProducer → retailer → consumer
Two-levelProducer → wholesaler → retailer → consumer
Three-levelProducer → wholesaler → jobber or agent → retailer → consumer
IntensityNumber of outletsTypical goods
IntensiveAs many as possibleConvenience goods: soap, biscuits, soft drinks
SelectiveMore than one but fewer than all willing dealersShopping goods: appliances, furniture
ExclusiveOne or very few dealers in each areaSpecialty and luxury goods: premium cars, designer labels

Don't confuse channel levels with distribution intensity. Levels count the intermediaries in the chain, its length. Intensity counts the outlets at the end of it, its breadth. A two-level channel can be intensive (biscuits) or selective (refrigerators). Also, merchants take title to the goods; agents do not.

Where it breaks. Each intermediary takes a margin, and the producer loses some control and direct contact with buyers. Selling online has removed some levels, but marketplaces and delivery firms have become new intermediaries.

For exams. Expect a path matched to its level, a product matched to its intensity, and merchants, agents and facilitators told apart by title and negotiation.

Direct or through intermediaries; intensive, selective or exclusive.

blocks.title: Channel systems and push and pull
blocks.html:
A paint maker's dealers want bigger margins, its distributors want faster payment, and each squeezes the others. When channel members pull apart like this, the customer pays for it in price or service.

In plain wordsA vertical marketing system is a channel whose members act as one team, not as separate businesses each chasing its own profit.

Exam definitionA vertical marketing system (VMS) comprises the producer, wholesaler(s) and retailer(s) acting as a unified system (Kotler and Keller).

In a conventional channel, producer, wholesaler and retailer are separate businesses, each maximising its own profit, often at the others' expense. That breeds conflict. A VMS removes it by ownership, contract or power.

KindHow the channel is unifiedIllustration
CorporateOne member owns the others, though each stage keeps its own taskA dairy that owns its chilling centres and its own milk parlours
ContractualIndependent firms join by contract: wholesaler-sponsored voluntary chains, retailer cooperatives (retailers buying through a jointly owned wholesaler) and franchise organisationsChemists in a city who jointly own the wholesaler they buy from
AdministeredOne member is large and powerful enough to coordinate the others without owning themA large consumer-goods maker that sets display and stocking terms for thousands of kirana stores

Franchises take three forms: manufacturer-sponsored retailer franchises (car dealers), manufacturer-sponsored wholesaler franchises (soft-drink bottlers licensed to bottle and distribute) and service-firm-sponsored retailer franchises (fast-food chains).

A VMS resembles vertical integration, in which a firm takes over the next link in the chain: forward toward customers or backward toward suppliers.

A horizontal marketing system joins two or more unrelated companies at the same level of the channel to exploit an opportunity. They pool capital, skills or marketing resources, often through a joint venture or alliance, temporary or permanent.

Multichannel (hybrid) marketing reaches customer segments through two or more channels at once: stores, websites, catalogues, direct mail, email and mobile.

StrategyHow it worksSuits
PushThe manufacturer uses its sales force and trade promotions to induce intermediaries to carry, promote and sell the productLow brand loyalty, brand chosen in the store, impulse items, well-understood benefits
PullThe manufacturer uses advertising and promotion to make consumers ask intermediaries for the productHigh brand loyalty and involvement, clear differences between brands, brand chosen before the store visit

A new snack brand might push, with extra margin and display money for kirana owners, since shoppers pick snacks at the counter. A phone brand pulls, with advertising, since buyers decide before they reach the shop. Most firms mix the two.

Reverse-flow channels move goods back from users to reuse products or containers, refurbish them for resale, recycle them, or dispose of products and packaging. They work through redemption centres, community groups, recycling centres and brokers. Service channels keep multiplying too: banks, insurers and travel firms serve customers through branches, phones and the internet. Performers and politicians reach their audiences through mass media, rallies, social networks and their own websites.

Don't confuse a horizontal marketing system with a merger. It is sometimes called a merger, but it is cooperation, and the firms usually stay separate. And keep the three franchise forms apart: most short accounts mention only the second, the bottler kind.

Where it breaks. An administered system lasts only as long as the leader's power. Multichannel selling brings conflict when a maker's own website undercuts its dealers. Pull needs heavy advertising that small firms cannot afford.

Conventional, vertical, horizontal, multichannel; push through the trade or pull through consumers.

blocks.title: Market logistics
blocks.html:
A shopper in Nagpur finds her usual detergent missing for a week, while the maker's warehouse in Mumbai is full of it. The product exists; logistics failed to put it where she buys.

In plain wordsMarket logistics is getting the right goods to the right place at the right time, at a cost that still leaves a profit.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: market logistics is planning, implementing and controlling the physical flow of materials, final goods and related information from points of origin to points of use, to meet customer requirements at a profit.

It is also called physical distribution or marketing logistics. Peter Drucker called distribution “the economy's dark continent” (1962) for the savings it hid. Kotler and Keller report that market logistics can amount to 30 to 40 per cent of a product's cost. So many experts call it ‘the last frontier for cost economies’: lower logistics costs allow lower prices, higher margins, or both.

TypeFlowAim
InboundRaw materials and inputs from suppliers to the factory and warehouse: procurement, receiving, storageSmooth production
OutboundFinished goods from the warehouse to customers and retailers: order processing, picking, packing, shippingCustomer satisfaction
ReverseReturns, recalls, repairs, recycling and excess stock back through the chainRecover value and build trust

Inbound logistics deals with supply; outbound logistics fulfils demand, usually through a warehouse management system. Reverse logistics is often handled as part of inbound.

The flow of market logistics. A sales forecast sets the schedules for distribution, production and inventory. Production plans tell purchasing what to order. Materials arrive by inbound transport, are stored, and are made into finished goods. Finished-goods inventory links customer orders to manufacturing. The goods then pass through packaging, warehousing, shipping, outbound transport, field warehousing and delivery.

DecisionKey question
Order processingHow quickly can we go from order to payment?
WarehousingHow many warehouses, and where?
InventoryWhen to reorder (the reorder point) and how much (the order quantity)?
TransportationWhich mode, judged by cost, speed and reliability?

Trade-offs. No system can both maximise service and minimise cost. Higher service needs more inventory and faster transport. Less inventory risks stockouts; cheaper packaging risks damage. Rail is cheaper than air but slower, which ties up working capital and delays payment. Because these costs pull in opposite directions, decisions must be made on a total-system basis. Start from what customers require and what competitors offer, and aim to maximise profit, not sales. Some firms offer less service at a lower price; others offer more service at a premium.

Planning. Kotler and Keller plan market logistics in four steps. First, decide the value proposition (delivery speed, accuracy, billing). Second, choose the channel design and network. Third, develop operational excellence in forecasting, warehousing, transport and materials. Fourth, implement with information systems, equipment, policies and continuous improvement. An integrated logistics system ties materials management, material flow and physical distribution together with point-of-sale data, barcodes, electronic data interchange (EDI), electronic funds transfer and satellite tracking.

Don't confuse physical distribution with supply chain management. Physical distribution starts at the factory gate: choosing stocking points and carriers. Supply chain management starts earlier, with buying the right inputs and converting them efficiently into finished products. Physical distribution has since grown into it.

Where it breaks. The 30 to 40 per cent figure is a broad estimate; the share differs widely between a bag of cement and a smartphone. Cutting one logistics cost often raises another, so a saving in one department can be a loss for the firm.

For exams. Expect Drucker's phrase, the three flows, and the total-system idea: no system both maximises service and minimises cost.

Right goods, right place, right time, lowest cost: trade-offs throughout.

blocks.title: The four logistics decisions
blocks.html:
A distributor of ceiling fans must decide when to reorder from the factory, and how many to order. Order too often and the paperwork and freight pile up; order too much and money sits in the godown.

In plain wordsLogistics comes down to four choices: how to handle orders, where to store, how much to hold, and how to ship.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the economic order quantity (EOQ) is the order size that minimises the total of ordering costs and inventory carrying costs.

DecisionWhat it involves
Order processingShortening the order-to-payment cycle: order transmission, order entry and credit check, inventory and production scheduling, shipping the order and invoice, and receiving payment. The longer the cycle, the lower customer satisfaction and profit.
WarehousingStoring goods because production and consumption rarely coincide. More stocking locations speed delivery but raise warehousing and inventory costs, so firms often centralise stock and use fast transport. Warehouses may be private or public; storage warehouses hold goods for moderate to long periods, while distribution warehouses move goods out as soon as possible; automated warehouses are run by a central computer. Some warehouses now assemble and pack, postponing final configuration to match demand more closely.
InventoryInventory cost rises at an accelerating rate as the service level approaches 100 per cent. The order (reorder) point balances the risk of stockout against the cost of overstock; the order quantity balances order-processing costs (set-up and running costs) against carrying costs (storage, capital, taxes and insurance, depreciation and obsolescence), which Kotler and Keller put as high as 30 per cent of inventory value. Larger stocks must earn incremental gross profit above their incremental carrying cost.
TransportationMode choice affects price, on-time delivery and the condition of goods. Shippers weigh speed, frequency, dependability, capability, availability, traceability and cost. For speed, air, rail and road lead; for low cost, water and pipeline.

The fan distributor, worked. Take illustrative figures: it sells 12,000 fans a year, about 40 a day over 300 working days. Each order costs ₹500 to place and receive, and holding one fan for a year costs ₹12.

EOQ = √(2 × annual demand × cost per order ÷ carrying cost per unit) = √(2 × 12,000 × ₹500 ÷ ₹12) = √10,00,000 = 1,000 fans

So it orders 1,000 fans, 12 times a year. Check: ordering costs 12 × ₹500 = ₹6,000; carrying costs, on an average stock of 500 fans, 500 × ₹12 = ₹6,000. At the EOQ the two are equal.

Reorder point = daily demand × lead time + safety stock = 40 × 5 days + 100 = 300 fans

With a 5-day lead time and 100 fans of safety stock, it reorders when stock falls to 300.

CarrierMeaning
PrivateThe shipper owns its own fleet of trucks or aircraft
ContractAn independent firm selling transport to others on contract
CommonA carrier serving set routes on a schedule, open to all shippers at standard rates

Don't confuse the reorder point with the order quantity. The reorder point says when to order (at 300 fans); the order quantity says how many (1,000). Also keep storage warehouses, which hold goods for long periods, apart from distribution warehouses, which move them out fast.

Where it breaks. The EOQ assumes steady demand and fixed costs. Seasonal peaks, such as fan sales before summer, break that assumption. Safety stock only covers the delays a firm expects.

For exams. Expect the four decisions, the two inventory questions (when and how much), the kinds of carrier, and an EOQ calculation.

Order processing, warehousing, inventory, transportation.

blocks.title: Supply chain management
blocks.html:
A phone brand runs out of its best seller during a Diwali sale because a chip supplier two steps back could not keep up. No single firm's logistics failed; the chain as a whole did.

In plain wordsA supply chain is every firm and step from raw material to the buyer's hands; managing it means running them as one.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a supply chain is the connected network of people, organisations, resources, activities and technologies involved in making and selling a product, from raw materials to the final consumer.

Supply chain management (SCM) coordinates these activities, streamlining the supply side to maximise customer value and gain competitive advantage. Controlling manufacturing improves quality and reduces the risk of recalls and lawsuits. Controlling shipping avoids costly shortages and oversupply.

AspectLogisticsSupply chain management (SCM)
ScopeMovement and storage of goods, mainly within one organisationThe whole chain from procurement through manufacturing to distribution
RelationA part of SCMThe wider whole
CoordinationInternalAcross many organisations
GoalEfficient logistics operations and customer satisfactionCompetitive advantage through an efficient, responsive chain
OriginThe older conceptThe newer, wider concept that grew out of logistics

The Supply Chain Council's SCOR model names five core processes: plan, source, make, deliver and return. For an auto-parts plant in Pune: plan output against car makers' schedules; source steel and castings; make the parts; deliver them to assembly lines; and take back defective parts.

Responsive or efficient. Michael Hugos describes five drivers. Each can be set for responsiveness, serving changing demand fast, or for efficiency, serving it at low cost. A fashion retailer leans to the first; a cement maker to the second.

DriverFor responsivenessFor efficiency
ProductionExcess capacity, flexible methods, many smaller plantsLittle excess capacity, specialised plants
InventoryHigh stock of a wide rangeLow stock of a narrower range
LocationMany facilities close to customersFew central facilities serving wide areas
TransportationFrequent shipments by fast, flexible modesFewer, larger shipments by slower, cheaper modes
InformationTimely, accurate data shared widelyLower information costs

Good SCM improves quality and customer service, reduces risk, raises profitability, and helps suppliers and buyers innovate together. Green supply chain practices include route optimisation, consolidating shipments, recyclable packaging and cutting the carbon footprint.

Don't confuse supply chain management with logistics. Logistics moves and stores goods, mainly inside one firm. SCM coordinates every firm in the chain, from buying inputs to returns. Logistics is one part of it.

Where it breaks. No chain can be fully responsive and fully efficient at once; each driver trades one against the other. Tight coordination also means dependence: a single supplier's failure can stop the whole chain.

For exams. Expect SCOR's five processes in order, Hugos' five drivers, and the logistics–SCM comparison. Later versions of SCOR add a sixth process, enable, but the classic answer is the five.

Go deeper for practitioners

The bullwhip effect. Small changes in consumer demand grow into larger swings in orders as they pass back up the chain, from retailer to distributor to factory to supplier. Hau Lee, V. Padmanabhan and Seungjin Whang (1997) traced it to four causes: each stage updating its own forecast, ordering in batches, buying ahead of price changes, and over-ordering when supplies are rationed.

The cure is shared information. When the factory sees actual sales at the till, not only its distributors' orders, it can plan to real demand. Smaller, more frequent orders and steady prices also damp the swings.

A decision. Your distributors' orders for a ₹2,000 mixer swing widely from month to month, while shop sales are steady. Before adding factory capacity, ask whether the swings come from demand or from how the chain orders.

Plan, source, make, deliver, return; responsive or efficient.

text: The Arthaśāstra's superintendent of the storehouse is told to keep half of the stored stock in reserve against calamities for the people, to use the other half, and to replace old stock with new. Safety stock and stock rotation are the same disciplines in modern inventory management.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.15

text: Kauṭilya compares trade routes. Earlier teachers preferred water routes as cheaper and easier; Kauṭilya prefers land routes as less liable to obstruction and danger, and among land routes he prefers the southern one for the goods it yields in quantity. Weighing routes by cost, risk and what they deliver is the same reasoning as a supply chain's choice of transport.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 7.12

text: The Jain Tattvārtha Sūtra states that living beings render service to one another. Supply chain management rests on a commercial version of the same idea: suppliers, makers and distributors do better by coordinating than by squeezing each other. The sūtra is a statement about all life, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Living beings render service to one another.” परस्परोपग्रहो जीवानाम् । parasparopagraho jīvānām. Umāsvāti, Tattvārtha Sūtra 5.21

chapters.title: Promotion Decisions: The Communication Mix and Budget
chapters.scope: The tools a firm uses to communicate with its market, how they are combined, and how the budget is set.

blocks.title: The promotion mix
blocks.html:
A new masala brand from Indore has ₹50 lakh to make itself known. It could run TV ads, give free samples in kirana stores, send salespeople to distributors, or set up a stall at a food fest. Choosing and combining these is the promotion decision.

In plain wordsThe promotion mix is the set of tools a firm uses to talk to its market, and the way it combines them.

Exam definitionMarketing communications are the means by which firms attempt to inform, persuade and remind consumers, directly or indirectly, about the products and brands they sell (Kotler and Keller).

Marketing communications are the voice of the company and its brands, and a way to build a dialogue with consumers. The promotion mix (marketing communications mix) is the blend of tools used for this. Its objectives are to inform, persuade, remind and, in social causes, modify behaviour.

ToolMeaningStrengths
AdvertisingAny paid form of non-personal presentation of ideas, goods or services by an identified sponsorReaches large audiences at low cost per exposure; builds image
Sales promotionShort-term incentives to encourage purchase: coupons, discounts, contests, samplesQuick response; boosts short-term sales
Personal sellingPersonal presentation by the sales force to make sales and build relationshipsTwo-way, adaptable; best at the stage of conviction and purchase
Public relationsBuilding good relations with the public through publicity, events and handling of storiesCredible; reaches people who avoid advertising
Direct and digital marketingDirect connections with targeted individuals: mail, email, phone, SMS, online and mobileTargeted, immediate, measurable

For the masala brand, ads build awareness and free sachets in kirana stores win trial. Salespeople persuade distributors to stock it, and a cooking contest at a food fest earns press coverage.

Kotler and Keller (14th edition) list eight modes: advertising, sales promotion, events and experiences, public relations and publicity, direct marketing, interactive (online) marketing, word-of-mouth marketing and personal selling. Later editions fold the online modes into online and social media marketing and mobile marketing.

Integrated marketing communications (IMC) is, in the AMA's definition, “a planning process designed to assure that all brand contacts received by a customer or prospect for a product, service, or organization are relevant to that person and consistent over time”. It takes a ‘360-degree view’ of the consumer and makes someone responsible for unifying the brand's messages. Integrated marketing, more broadly, designs every activity with all the others in mind, so that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.

Push and pull. A firm can promote through the channel or around it.

StrategyHow it worksMain tools
PushThe producer promotes to channel members, who promote to final buyersPersonal selling and trade promotion
PullThe producer promotes to final consumers, who ask channel members for the productAdvertising and consumer promotion

AIDA (attention, interest, desire, action), usually credited to E. St. Elmo Lewis (1898), is the oldest model of how buyers respond to communication.

Don't confuse the promotion mix with the marketing mix. Promotion is one of the 4Ps; the promotion mix is the set of tools inside that one P. Likewise, sales promotion is one tool in the promotion mix, not another name for it.

Where it breaks. The tools overlap: an influencer's post is digital marketing and word of mouth at once. IMC is hard to run when different agencies and departments own different tools.

For exams. Expect the definition of each tool, push matched with personal selling and trade promotion, pull with advertising and consumer promotion, and AIDA with Lewis.

Advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, PR, direct marketing.

blocks.title: Developing effective communications
blocks.html:
A public-sector bank launches a mobile app and wants pensioners to use it. A clever ad on the wrong channel, or aimed at the wrong person, will be wasted. Effective communication is planned in steps, starting with who must hear it.

The rule is to plan backwards: decide whom to reach and what they should do, then what to say, who says it, and where. The standard sequence has seven steps.

StepWhat it involves
1 Identify the target audiencePotential buyers, current users, deciders and influencers; individuals, groups, particular publics or the general public
2 Determine the objectivesCategory need, brand awareness, brand attitude or purchase intention (see below)
3 Design the communicationsWhat to say (message strategy), how to say it (creative strategy) and who should say it (message source)
4 Select the channelsPersonal and non-personal channels
5 Establish the total budgetAffordable, percentage-of-sales, competitive-parity or objective-and-task
6 Decide on the communications mixAllocate the budget across the modes
7 Measure results and manage IMCCheck effects and keep the messages integrated

The bank, step by step. The audience is pensioners, with their grown-up children as influencers. The first objective is awareness, then purchase intention: downloading the app. The message stresses safety and ease; a demonstration ad shows a pension being checked in three taps. The source is a branch manager customers already trust. Channels are branch posters and staff (personal), plus SMS and newspapers (non-personal).

ObjectiveMeaning
Category needEstablish the need for the category, as any new-to-the-world product such as early electric cars must
Brand awarenessHelp consumers recognise or recall the brand within the category; recognition is easier to achieve than recall
Brand attitudeHelp consumers judge the brand's ability to meet a relevant need: problem-solution appeals for cleaning products, sensory appeals for foods
Brand purchase intentionMove consumers to decide to buy, or to take a purchase-related action

Message, creative and source. The message strategy looks for appeals and themes that tie to the brand's positioning and its points of parity and difference. Creative strategy uses informational appeals, which elaborate on attributes and benefits (problem-solution, demonstration, comparison and testimonial ads). Or it uses transformational appeals, which elaborate on a non-product benefit or image, such as what kind of person uses the brand. Attractive or popular sources win more attention and recall, which is why firms use celebrities.

ChannelForms
PersonalTwo or more people communicating directly, face to face, by phone or online, allowing individual presentation and feedback: advocate channels (company salespeople), expert channels (independent experts) and social channels (neighbours, friends, family)
Non-personal (mass)Communications directed to more than one person: media (print, broadcast, electronic, display), atmospheres (packaged environments that reinforce leanings toward a product) and events

Don't confuse informational with transformational appeals. Informational appeals argue from the product: what it does and why it is better. Transformational appeals argue from feelings and image: who you become by using it. A demonstration is informational even when it is entertaining.

Where it breaks. The steps look like a straight line, but in practice the budget often limits the objectives, and results send planners back to the start. A famous source can also overshadow the brand, and the source's troubles become the brand's troubles.

In practice. Start from the audience and the objective, not from a favourite medium. Choose the source the audience trusts, not the one the firm admires.

Audience, objectives, design, channels, budget, mix, results.

blocks.title: Setting the promotion budget
blocks.html:
A snack maker in Pune must decide how much to spend on promotion next year. Four common methods give four answers, from ₹40 lakh to ₹1 crore.

In plain wordsThe promotion budget is the money set aside to communicate with the market, and the method is the logic used to arrive at it.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition of the objective-and-task method: define specific objectives, determine the tasks needed to achieve them, and estimate the cost of those tasks; the sum of the costs is the budget.

MethodHow it worksWeakness
AffordableSpend what the company thinks it can afford after other costsIgnores promotion's effect on sales; budget varies year to year
Percentage of salesSpend a set percentage of current or forecast salesTreats sales as the cause of promotion rather than its result
Competitive parityMatch competitors' spendingCompetitors' needs and wisdom may differ
Objective and taskDefine objectives, set the tasks to achieve them, cost the tasks; the total is the budgetDemanding to estimate, but the most logical

Work it out. An illustration: the snack maker forecasts sales of ₹24 crore next year.

  • Affordable: after all other costs and the profit the owners want, ₹40 lakh is left.
  • Percentage of sales: at 3% of forecast sales, 0.03 × ₹24 crore = ₹72 lakh.
  • Competitive parity: the main rival spends about ₹1 crore, so the firm matches it.
  • Objective and task: the objective is awareness among 30% of target buyers in Maharashtra, and stock in 10,000 shops. The tasks cost ₹45 lakh for a regional ad campaign, ₹15 lakh for sampling, ₹12 lakh for display allowances to shops, and ₹3 lakh to measure awareness. Total: 45 + 15 + 12 + 3 = ₹75 lakh.

In competitive parity, firms aim at share-of-voice parity with rivals. Share of voice is a brand's promotion spending as a share of all promotion spending in its category. If the whole category spends ₹5 crore, the rival's ₹1 crore is a 20% share of voice (1 ÷ 5 = 0.2).

Don't confuse share of voice with market share. Share of voice measures a brand's share of the category's promotion; market share measures its share of the category's sales. A small brand can shout loudly and still sell little.

Where it breaks. The difficulty is captured in a saying usually credited to the retailer John Wanamaker: half the money spent on advertising is wasted; the trouble is knowing which half. Objective and task is the most logical method, but it assumes the firm knows what each task will achieve, which is the hard part.

For exams. Objective and task is “the most logical”; percentage of sales “treats sales as the cause of promotion”; affordable “ignores promotion's effect on sales”; competitive parity uses share of voice.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. Sales fall 10% in a slow year. Under percentage of sales, the budget falls 10% too, just when the brand may need support. Under objective and task, the question is different: which tasks still matter, and what do they cost? The answer may be a smaller budget, but it is reasoned, not automatic.

Combining methods. A firm can build the budget by objective and task, then check it against percentage of sales (can we carry it?) and share of voice (will we be heard?). Sharp disagreement suggests unrealistic objectives.

Objective and task is the most logical method.

blocks.title: Advertising
blocks.html:
A regional two-wheeler brand books ads on cricket broadcasts before Diwali. Should it show the ad once to many people, or many times to fewer? What should the ad try to do? Advertising decisions answer such questions in order.

In plain wordsAdvertising is a message a firm pays to place in a medium, openly in its own name, to reach many people at once.

Exam definitionAdvertising is any paid form of non-personal presentation and promotion of ideas, goods or services by an identified sponsor (Kotler and Keller).

Advertising reaches scattered buyers, builds a long-term image or triggers quick sales. Its qualities are public presentation, pervasiveness (the message can be repeated many times), amplified expressiveness (dramatising the brand through print, sound and colour), impersonality, and control over what the message stresses.

Its forms include print and broadcast ads, outer packaging and inserts, cinema, posters and leaflets, brochures, directories, billboards, point-of-purchase displays, advertorials, infomercials, and online banner, video and social media ads.

MDecision
MissionSetting the objectives
MoneyDeciding the budget
MessageGenerating, evaluating and executing the message, and checking its social responsibility
MediaChoosing reach, frequency and impact, the media types and vehicles, and timing
MeasurementEvaluating the communication and sales effects
KindAimTwo-wheeler example
InformativeCreate awareness and knowledge of new products or featuresA new model with better mileage is launched
PersuasiveCreate liking, preference, conviction and purchaseWhy this model beats its rivals
ReminderStimulate repeat purchaseThe brand's name shown during the festive season
ReinforcementConvince current buyers they made the right choiceHappy owners describe two years of trouble-free riding

Budget factors: the stage in the product life cycle, market share and consumer base, competition and clutter, the advertising frequency needed, and how substitutable the product is. Although treated as a current expense, part of advertising is an investment in brand equity.

Media. Media selection finds the most cost-effective media to deliver the desired number and type of exposures. Three measures matter: reach (how many people are exposed at least once), frequency (how often the average person is exposed) and impact (the qualitative value of an exposure). Reach times frequency gives gross rating points (GRPs), the total weight of a schedule.

GRPs = reach (% of target audience) × average frequency

If the cricket ads reach 60% of the target audience an average of 4 times, the schedule delivers 60 × 4 = 240 GRPs. Reaching 40% six times also gives 240 GRPs, to fewer people, more often.

As traditional mass media lose effectiveness, advertisers use more alternative media. Effectiveness is measured both as a communication effect (on awareness, knowledge or preference) and as a sales effect.

Don't confuse advertising with publicity. Advertising is paid for, carries the sponsor's name and says what the sponsor chooses. Publicity is coverage the firm does not pay for and does not control, which is why it is more credible. Also keep reminder (buy again) apart from reinforcement (you chose well).

Where it breaks. Sales effects are hard to measure, because price, distribution and competitors move sales too. Clutter and ad-skipping weaken each exposure.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision: reach or frequency? With a fixed budget, more of one means less of the other. Kotler and Keller's guidance: reach matters most when launching new products, brand extensions or flanker brands, or when the target market is not well defined. Frequency matters most when competitors are strong, the story is complex, buyers resist the message, or the product is bought often.

For the two-wheeler brand launching a new model, that points to reach first; for an established brand in a crowded festive season, frequency may matter more.

Mission, money, message, media, measurement.

blocks.title: Sales promotion and personal selling
blocks.html:
A supermarket's Diwali offer, ‘buy two, get one free’, empties a shelf in a week. A machine-tool maker in Pune spends six months and many visits to sell one ₹50 lakh machine. Both are promotion, working in opposite ways.

In plain wordsSales promotion gives people a reason to buy now; personal selling is a salesperson persuading a buyer, usually face to face.

Exam definitionSales promotion consists of a collection of incentive tools, mostly short term, designed to stimulate quicker or greater purchase of particular products or services by consumers or the trade (Kotler and Keller).

Sales promotion has three targets: consumer promotions, trade promotions, and business and sales-force promotions. It offers three benefits: it draws attention, gives an incentive, and makes an invitation to buy now.

Why it has grown: the growing power of retailers, declining brand loyalty, consumers' greater sensitivity to promotions, the proliferation of brands, fragmented markets, a short-term focus, demands for measurable results, and competition.

ToolWhat it is
SamplesA free amount of the product, delivered, mailed, picked up or attached to another product
CouponsCertificates entitling the bearer to a stated saving
Cash refunds (rebates)A price reduction after purchase, on proof of purchase
Price packsReduced-price packs (two for the price of one) or banded packs (a toothbrush with toothpaste)
PremiumsMerchandise free or at low cost as an incentive to buy
Frequency programmesRewards linked to how often and how much a customer buys
PrizesContests (judged entries), sweepstakes (draws) and games
Patronage awardsValue in proportion to patronage, such as reward points
Free trials, warrantiesTrying the product at no cost; promises of performance or refund
Tie-ins and cross-promotionsBrands teaming up on offers, or one brand advertising a non-competing brand
Point-of-purchase displays and demonstrationsAt the place of sale
ToolWhat it is
Price-off (off-invoice)A straight discount off the list price on each case bought in a stated period
AllowancePayment for featuring the product: an advertising allowance, or a display allowance for a special display
Free goodsExtra cases for intermediaries who buy a certain quantity

Work it out: what ‘buy two, get one free’ costs. An illustration: a pack sells for ₹60 and costs the seller ₹35, a margin of ₹25. On the offer, the buyer pays ₹120 for three packs, or ₹40 a pack: a price cut of one-third. The cost of three packs is ₹105, so profit is ₹15 for three, or ₹5 a pack. To earn the same profit as before, the seller must sell five times as many packs (₹25 ÷ ₹5 = 5).

Personal selling is the personal presentation by a firm's sales force to make sales and build customer relationships.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Two-way: instant feedback lets the seller adapt the presentationExpensive per contact
Builds trust, which matters for high-value productsLabour-intensive; needs a large sales force
More persuasive: a buyer face to face is less likely to dismiss the sellerTraining is slow and costly
Reaches buyers other methods cannotReaches relatively few people

Don't confuse sales promotion with advertising. Advertising gives a reason to buy; sales promotion gives an incentive to buy now. Also: a contest judges entries, a sweepstakes draws names; a price pack cuts the price on the pack, a coupon is a certificate for a stated saving.

Where it breaks. Frequent deals can teach buyers to wait for the next one and can cheapen a brand, and the arithmetic above shows how fast they eat margin.

In practice. Use sales promotion, for a limited time, to win trial or clear stock. Use personal selling where the product is costly, complex or made to order.

Sales promotion buys action now; personal selling builds conviction one buyer at a time.

text: Advertising aims to hold its audience and reach even those not yet listening. The Kuṟaḷ describes true speech as speech that binds its hearers and makes even those who were not listening want to hear. It is about eloquence, not paid media.
pairings.quote: “True speech binds those who hear it and makes even those who did not hear it long for it.” கேட்டார்ப் பிணிக்கும் தகையவாய்க் கேளாரும் வேட்ப மொழிவதாம் சொல். Tirukkuṟaḷ 643

text: The affordable method sets spending by what the firm can bear. The Kuṟaḷ says to give according to the measure of one's means: that is the way to give while keeping one's wealth. The couplet concerns a ruler's or householder's gifts, not a promotion budget.
pairings.quote: “Give with knowledge of the measure of your means; that is the way to give while guarding your wealth.” ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து ஈக அதுபொருள் போற்றி வழங்கு நெறி. Tirukkuṟaḷ 477

chapters.title: Consumer and Industrial Buying Behaviour
chapters.scope: Why and how people and organisations buy: the influences on them, the decision process, the rules they use, and how business buying differs.

blocks.title: Consumer behaviour and its influences
blocks.html:
Two families in Lucknow with the same income walk into the same showroom and leave with different scooters. Price alone does not explain it. Consumer behaviour studies what does.

In plain wordsConsumer behaviour is how people choose, buy, use and get rid of things, and why.

Exam definitionConsumer behaviour is the study of how individuals, groups and organisations select, buy, use and dispose of goods, services, ideas or experiences to satisfy their needs and wants (Kotler and Keller).

Leon Schiffman and Leslie Lazar Kanuk define it as the behaviour consumers display in searching for, purchasing, using, evaluating and disposing of products and services that they expect will satisfy their needs. It draws on psychology, sociology, anthropology and economics, and is complex, dynamic, goal-oriented and shaped by perception.

An example. A family buys a scooter for a daughter starting college. Its region and class shape what seems normal (cultural). Her friends' scooters and her parents' views count (social). She is a student on a set budget (personal). She wants safety and style, and has a picture of each brand in her mind (psychological).

FactorVariablesNotes
CulturalCulture, subculture, social classCulture is the most basic cause of wants; subcultures (ethnic, religious, regional) form niche markets; class shapes lifestyle and access
SocialReference groups, family, roles and statusPrimary groups (family, friends) and secondary groups (professional bodies) shape attitudes; buying roles are initiator, influencer, decider, buyer and user
PersonalAge and life-cycle stage, occupation, economic situation, lifestyle, personality and self-conceptLifestyle is measured by activities, interests and opinions (AIO)
PsychologicalMotivation, perception, learning, beliefs and attitudesMaslow's and Herzberg's theories; selective attention, distortion and retention; learning by experience; attitudes are lasting and hard to change

In the scooter purchase, the daughter is the initiator and the user, her friends are influencers, her father is the decider, and her mother, who goes to the showroom and pays, is the buyer.

Don't confuse the buyer with the user or the decider. The person who pays is often not the person who chooses or the person who uses. Marketers must find out who plays each role, because each needs a different message.

Where it breaks. The four factors act together, and the list explains a purchase after it happens better than it predicts the next one.

For exams. Culture is the most basic cause of wants; lifestyle is measured by AIO; the five buying roles belong to the social factors.

Cultural, social, personal, psychological.

blocks.title: The buying decision process
blocks.html:
Nobody compares brands before buying a packet of biscuits, but most people do before buying a refrigerator. The buying decision process maps the steps of a considered purchase, and shows where a seller can win or lose the sale.

In plain wordsThe buying decision process is the path from noticing a need to judging the purchase afterwards.

Exam definitionA standard textbook model: the consumer passes through five stages, need recognition, information search, evaluation of alternatives, purchase decision and post-purchase behaviour; buying starts before the purchase and continues after it.

StageWhat happens
1 Need recognitionThe buyer recognises a gap between the actual and the desired state, triggered by internal stimuli (hunger) or external ones (an advertisement)
2 Information searchInternal search of memory and experience; external search among family, friends, experts, reviews and advertising
3 Evaluation of alternativesComparing options on criteria such as price, brand, features and quality, within the evoked set
4 Purchase decisionForming an intention and buying; others' attitudes and unexpected situations can intervene
5 Post-purchase behaviourSatisfaction leads to repurchase and loyalty; dissatisfaction to returns and complaints

An example. Ravi's old refrigerator breaks down before Diwali. He recalls brands he has owned, then asks his sister and reads reviews. He compares three models around ₹30,000 on price, capacity and power use. He picks one, but his brother says another brand is better, and he almost changes his mind. A week after buying, he wonders if he chose well, until the brand calls to check the installation.

The evoked set. From the total set of brands available, a buyer is aware of some (the awareness set), considers fewer (the consideration or evoked set), and chooses among a few (the choice set). Ravi might know 8 of 20 brands on sale, consider 3, and choose between the last 2.

Cognitive dissonance (Leon Festinger, 1957) is the discomfort after purchase caused by doubt about the choice, often called buyer's remorse. Marketers reduce it with reassurance, guarantees and after-sales contact. Satisfaction depends on the gap between expectations and perceived performance.

Involvement decides how much of this process a buyer goes through, from routine to extensive decisions.

Don't confuse cognitive dissonance with dissatisfaction. Dissatisfaction means the product performed below expectations. Dissonance is doubt about the choice, and it can arise even when the product works well, because the rejected options also had attractions.

Where it breaks. The model describes a considered purchase. Impulse buys skip stages, and routine buys jump from need straight to purchase.

In practice. Each stage is a point of action: ads trigger need, reviews feed the search, comparisons shape evaluation, offers close the sale, and follow-up calls ease dissonance.

Need, search, evaluate, buy, reflect.

blocks.title: Types of buying behaviour
blocks.html:
A buyer may spend weeks choosing a car and two seconds choosing salt. A marketer who treats the two alike wastes money on one and loses sales on the other.

In plain wordsInvolvement is how much a purchase matters to the buyer: its cost, its risk and what it says about them.

Exam definitionHenry Assael classified buying behaviour into four types by two dimensions: the buyer's degree of involvement, and the degree of difference between brands.

Brand differencesHigh involvementLow involvement
Significant differences between brandsComplex buying: buying a car. The marketer gives detailed information and trials.Variety-seeking: soft drinks, biscuits. Buyers switch for variety; leaders keep shelf space and remind, challengers offer deals and novelty.
Few differences between brandsDissonance-reducing: buying a carpet. The marketer provides reassurance and after-sales support.Habitual: salt. Buyers buy by habit; marketers use price, promotion and repetition to build familiarity.

Reading the grid. A carpet costs a lot, so involvement is high, but many carpets look alike. The buyer decides fairly quickly, often on price or convenience, then looks for signs the choice was right. That is why the marketer's job comes after the sale: reassurance.

Don't confuse dissonance-reducing with complex buying. Both are high involvement. In complex buying the brands differ, so the buyer studies them first. In dissonance-reducing buying they look alike, so the buyer decides quickly and seeks comfort afterwards. Variety-seeking is also not dissatisfaction: the buyer switches for a change, not because the last brand failed.

Where it breaks. Involvement belongs to the buyer, not the product. A tea lover may study tea blends as carefully as a car, while a busy buyer reorders the same car brand by habit.

For exams. Expect a product to place in the grid, or a marketing response to match to a type.

High involvement and real differences make buying complex.

blocks.title: Decision rules and models of buyer behaviour
blocks.html:
Three phones, three buyers, three different choices, even with the same ratings in front of them. The difference is the rule each buyer uses to turn ratings into a decision.

In plain wordsA decision rule is the shortcut a buyer uses to pick one brand from several.

Exam definitionA standard textbook distinction: under non-compensatory rules, a weakness on one attribute cannot be offset by strength on another; under compensatory rules, it can.

RuleHow the buyer choosesMarketing implication
ConjunctiveSets a minimum acceptable level on every attribute and chooses the first brand that meets all of themMake sure the product meets the minimum on everything
DisjunctiveSets a high standard on one or a few key attributes and accepts a brand that meets any of themHighlight a standout feature
LexicographicRanks the attributes and compares brands on the most important first, moving to the next only if there is a tieExcel on the attribute buyers rank first

Under compensatory rules, such as Martin Fishbein's expectancy-value model, a buyer weighs all attributes together, so strengths can offset weaknesses.

Work it out. An illustration: phones A, B and C are rated out of 10. The buyer's weights are price 0.4, battery 0.3, camera 0.3.

PhonePriceBatteryCameraWeighted score
A9553.6 + 1.5 + 1.5 = 6.6
B6882.4 + 2.4 + 2.4 = 7.2
C7942.8 + 2.7 + 1.2 = 6.7
  • Compensatory: B has the highest weighted score, 7.2.
  • Lexicographic, price first: A wins, with 9 on price.
  • Conjunctive, minimum 5 on everything: C fails on camera; A and B pass, and the buyer takes whichever is met first.
  • Disjunctive, battery of 9 or more: only C qualifies.
TypeExplains buying by…
Economic (Marshallian)Rational choice to maximise satisfaction within a budget
PsychologicalLearning and conditioning (Pavlovian), unconscious motives (Freudian), needs (Maslow)
Sociological (Veblenian)Family, social class, reference groups and culture
ComprehensiveCombining these: the Nicosia model (1966), the Engel–Kollat–Blackwell model (1968) and the Howard–Sheth model (1969)

Don't confuse conjunctive with disjunctive. Conjunctive means “and”: every attribute must pass its minimum. Disjunctive means “or”: passing a high standard on any key attribute is enough.

Where it breaks. Real buyers mix rules: they often screen out brands with a conjunctive cut-off, then weigh the survivors compensatorily. The models are frameworks for thinking, not formulas that predict a purchase.

In practice. Find out which rule your buyers use. If they screen on a minimum, a single weak attribute can remove you before your strengths are seen.

Go deeper for practitioners

The comprehensive models. Each tries to show the whole decision in one diagram. The Nicosia model traces a message from the firm to the consumer's attitude, then through search and evaluation, purchase, and feedback. The Howard–Sheth model links inputs (stimuli from products and the social environment) through perceptual and learning constructs to outputs, from attention to purchase. The Engel–Kollat–Blackwell model centres on the five-stage decision process, fed by information processing and outside influences.

A decision. Your phone scores well overall but is the most expensive. If research shows buyers rank price first (lexicographic), cutting the price matters more than another camera upgrade. If they weigh everything (compensatory), the upgrade may be enough.

Links. The five-stage process in this chapter is where these rules operate: they are how stage 3, evaluation of alternatives, ends.

Conjunctive: every minimum. Disjunctive: one high standard. Lexicographic: the top attribute first.

blocks.title: Industrial (organisational) buying behaviour
blocks.html:
An auto-parts plant in Pune reorders bolts with one email, but buying its first welding robot takes months and a dozen people. Selling to organisations means knowing which kind of purchase it is, and who is involved.

In plain wordsOrganisational buying is how a company, hospital or government office decides what to buy and from whom.

Exam definitionOrganisational buying is the decision-making process by which formal organisations establish the need for purchased products and services, and identify, evaluate and choose among alternative brands and suppliers (Frederick Webster and Yoram Wind).

How business markets differ: fewer, larger buyers; close supplier-customer relationships; professional purchasing by trained buyers; several people influencing each decision; and geographically concentrated buyers. Above all, derived demand: demand for business goods comes from demand for the consumer goods they help produce. It is fairly inelastic in the short run and fluctuates more. If car sales fall, the Pune plant's orders for steel and parts fall with them, whatever the steel price.

BuyclassWhat happensRiskAt the Pune plant
Straight rebuyRoutine reorder from an established supplier with little evaluationLowReordering bolts
Modified rebuyThe buyer re-evaluates products, prices or suppliers because needs have changedMediumSeeking new paint suppliers after a price rise
New taskA first-time purchase needing extensive research and many decision-makersHighBuying the first welding robot

The buyclasses and the buygrid come from Patrick Robinson, Charles Faris and Yoram Wind (Industrial Buying and Creative Marketing, 1967). The buygrid crosses the three buyclasses with eight buyphases: problem recognition, general need description, product specification, supplier search, proposal solicitation, supplier selection, order-routine specification, and performance review. A new task goes through all eight; a straight rebuy skips most of them.

The buying centre is everyone involved in a purchase decision. Webster and Wind (1972) named five roles: users, influencers, buyers, deciders and gatekeepers (who control the flow of information); later writers add initiators and approvers. For the robot: the shop-floor supervisor who will run it is a user; the production engineer who writes the specification is an influencer; the purchase officer who negotiates is the buyer, and also a gatekeeper who decides which sellers reach the engineers; the plant head is the decider.

Webster and Wind's model groups the influences on organisational buying into four kinds: environmental, organisational, interpersonal and individual.

Don't confuse the buyer with the decider. The buyer has formal authority to choose suppliers and arrange terms. The decider has the power to settle the choice, and in a big purchase that is often someone more senior.

Where it breaks. The buygrid describes a tidy, rational sequence. Real purchases also run on trust, past relationships and internal politics, which the framework names but cannot measure.

For exams. Match the buyclasses and buygrid to Robinson, Faris and Wind (1967), and the buying centre and four influences to Webster and Wind (1972). Derived demand is the classic contrast with consumer markets.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. You sell welding robots and have reached the Pune plant's purchase officer. Do you keep selling to him? The buying-centre view says map every role first. The engineer sets the specification, so make sure your robot meets it. The supervisor will use it, so a demonstration may win an ally. The plant head decides, so prepare the cost and payback case for that level.

Buyclass changes the job. As the current supplier in a straight rebuy, protect the routine: deliver on time and give no reason to re-evaluate. As an outside supplier, try to turn a straight rebuy into a modified rebuy by offering something new.

Straight rebuy, modified rebuy, new task.

text: The Kuṟaḷ says that just as water changes its nature with the soil it flows through, people's understanding takes on the nature of the company they keep. That is the reference group effect: the groups we belong to and look to shape what we think and want.
pairings.quote: “As water changes with the nature of the soil, so a person's understanding takes the nature of their company.” நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர்திரிந் தற்றாகும் மாந்தர்க்கு இனத்தியல்ப தாகும் அறிவு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 452

text: Cognitive dissonance is regret after a choice. The Kuṟaḷ warns against doing what will later make one cry, ‘what have I done?’, and if it has been done, not to do it again. It speaks of wrong actions generally, not purchases.
pairings.quote: “Do nothing that will make you grieve, ‘what have I done!’; and if you have, better not do such things again.” எற்றென்று இரங்குவ செய்யற்க செய்வானேல் மற்றன்ன செய்யாமை நன்று. Tirukkuṟaḷ 655

text: The Arthaśāstra devotes a chapter to examining precious goods, gems, pearls and the like, before they are accepted into the treasury, with their qualities and defects set out so that experts can judge them. Professional, specification-based examination of what an organisation buys is the same practice in an industrial buying centre.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.11

chapters.title: Services Marketing
chapters.scope: How services differ from goods, the extended marketing mix, how service quality is measured, and the three kinds of services marketing.

blocks.title: Services and their characteristics
blocks.html:
A service is any act or performance one party offers another that is essentially intangible and does not result in the ownership of anything (Kotler). Services marketing creates value through experiences, processes and interactions; it is relationship-oriented, and customer interaction is critical.

CharacteristicMeaningExampleMarketing response
IntangibilityCannot be seen, tasted, felt or heard before purchaseInsurance, legal adviceMake it tangible with evidence: facilities, staff, testimonials
InseparabilityProduced and consumed at the same time; the provider is part of the serviceA doctor's consultationTrain the people who deliver it; manage customers' participation
Variability (heterogeneity)Quality depends on who provides it, when, where and howRestaurant serviceStandardise processes, train staff, track satisfaction
PerishabilityCannot be stored for later sale or use; unused capacity is lostEmpty airline seatsMatch supply and demand: differential pricing, reservations, part-time staff
Lack of ownershipThe customer gets an experience or access, not ownershipEducation, tourismBuild membership and loyalty
CategoryExample
Pure tangible goodSoap, toothpaste or salt, with no accompanying service
Tangible good with accompanying servicesA car, computer or phone; the more advanced the product, the more it needs good support
HybridA restaurant meal: equal parts goods and service
Major service with accompanying minor goods and servicesAir travel, with snacks and drinks
Pure serviceBabysitting, psychotherapy, massage

Managing the characteristics. Because buyers cannot see a service in advance, they look for evidence of quality in the place, people, equipment, communication material, symbols and price, so the provider's task is to manage the evidence and ‘tangibilise the intangible’. Variability can be reduced in three steps: invest in good hiring and training, standardise the service process across the organisation, and monitor customer satisfaction; service guarantees reassure buyers. Perishability matters when demand fluctuates: transport firms must own enough equipment for rush hour, and some doctors charge for missed appointments. Demand or yield management aims to offer the right services to the right customers at the right places, times and prices.

Intangible, inseparable, variable, perishable, not owned.

blocks.title: The services marketing mix: 7Ps
blocks.html:
Bernard Booms and Mary Jo Bitner (1981) added three Ps to the four for services.

PFocusExample
ProductThe core and supplementary servicesA bank loan
PriceValue-based and flexible pricingA subscription fee
PlaceAccessibility and deliveryBranches and mobile apps
PromotionCommunicationAdvertising, public relations
PeopleEveryone who takes part in delivering the serviceReceptionists, agents
ProcessThe procedures and flow by which the service is deliveredA booking system
Physical evidenceThe setting and tangible cuesOffices, uniforms, brochures

The 4Ps plus people, process and physical evidence.

blocks.title: Service quality and SERVQUAL
blocks.html:
SERVQUAL (A. Parasuraman, Valarie Zeithaml and Leonard Berry, 1988) measures service quality as the gap between customers' expectations and their perceptions of performance, on five dimensions. It grew out of the same authors' gaps model (1985).

DimensionMeaningExample
ReliabilityPerforming the promised service dependably and accuratelyOn-time delivery
AssuranceEmployees' knowledge and courtesy, and their ability to convey trust and confidenceSkilled, courteous staff
TangiblesThe appearance of physical facilities, equipment, staff and materialsA modern office
EmpathyCaring, individual attentionPersonalised care
ResponsivenessWillingness to help customers and give prompt serviceQuick support
GapBetweenExample
1 Knowledge gapCustomers' expectations and management's perception of themA bank's managers think customers want better debit cards when they care more about staff responsiveness
2 Standards gapManagement's perceptions and the service quality specificationsManagers ask tellers for ‘fast’ service without saying how many minutes
3 Delivery gapThe specifications and the service actually deliveredStaff are poorly trained, or caught between standards such as listening to customers and serving them fast
4 Communication gapThe service delivered and what is promised to customersA hospital brochure shows a beautiful room; the patient finds a shabby one
5 Customer gapExpected and perceived service; the result of gaps 1 to 4A doctor's frequent visits, meant to show care, make the patient think something is wrong

Customers form expectations from past experience, word of mouth and advertising, and compare the service they perceive with the service they expected. Falling short disappoints; exceeding expectations delights. Kotler and Keller list the five dimensions in order of importance to customers: reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy, tangibles.

The zone of tolerance (Zeithaml, Berry and Parasuraman, 1993) is the range between the desired and the adequate service level, within which variation in service goes largely unnoticed.

ModelSatisfaction depends on…
Expectancy disconfirmation (Richard Oliver, 1980)Comparing performance with expectations: performance above expectation satisfies, below it dissatisfies
Performance-onlyPerformance alone; useful for new services where customers have few expectations
Rational expectationsExpectations formed by logical evaluation, then matched against performance
Expectations as artefactThe expectations themselves, which shape how performance is perceived; managing expectations improves satisfaction

Reliability, Assurance, Tangibles, Empathy, Responsiveness.

blocks.title: The service triangle
blocks.html:
The service triangle links the company, its employees and its customers. Each side is a kind of marketing, and all three are needed for good service.

KindBetweenFocus
Internal marketingCompany and employeesHiring, training and motivating staff to serve customers well; building a service culture
External marketingCompany and customersPreparing, pricing, distributing and promoting the service: making promises
Interactive marketingEmployees and customersThe service encounter, where promises are kept or broken and relationships are built

Kotler and Keller argue that the marketing department's most important contribution may be to be ‘exceptionally clever in getting everyone else in the organization to practice marketing’. In interactive marketing, clients judge both technical quality (was the surgery successful?) and functional quality (did the surgeon show concern and inspire confidence?).

Internal, external, interactive: promise, enable, deliver.

blocks.title: Excellence in services and service brands
blocks.html:
Well-managed service companies share several practices (Kotler and Keller).

PracticeWhat it means
A strategic conceptBeing ‘customer-obsessed’: a clear sense of target customers and their needs, and a distinctive strategy to satisfy them; very selective hiring; some hotels keep a ‘guest historian’ to track preferences
Top-management commitmentLooking at service performance as well as financial results; McDonald's measures every outlet on QSCV: quality, service, cleanliness and value
High standardsSetting precise, appropriately high standards, such as answering calls within a set number of seconds
Profit tiersPampering high-value customers and charging more or serving more economically those who barely pay their way
Monitoring systemsAuditing their own and competitors' service: voice-of-the-customer measures, comparison and mystery shopping, surveys, suggestion and complaint forms, service-audit teams
Satisfying complaintsKotler and Keller note that on average 40 per cent of customers who have a bad service experience stop doing business with the firm; a complaint handled well is a gift, and firms that encourage complaints and empower staff to fix problems on the spot earn more

Service brands. As firms move from making products to delivering solutions and services, they build service brands, which depend on consistently high delivery; a pure service brand, such as an airline, sells mainly a service. Marketers must turn intangible services into concrete benefits and a well-defined experience, as theme parks do. Brand experience has four dimensions: sensory, affective, behavioural and intellectual.

Customer-obsessed, committed, high standards, tiers, monitoring, complaints welcomed.

text: SERVQUAL's responsiveness is the willingness to help promptly. The Kuṟaḷ says that help given at the right time, however small, is greater than the world. It is about kindness between people, not about service firms.
pairings.quote: “Help given in time of need, though small in itself, is far greater than the world.” காலத்தி னாற்செய்த நன்றி சிறிதெனினும் ஞாலத்தின் மாணப் பெரிது. Tirukkuṟaḷ 102

text: Interactive marketing happens in the moment of contact. The Kuṟaḷ says the anicham flower withers when smelt, but a guest withers at a mere cold look. It concerns a host's hospitality, which is also the root idea of the service encounter.
pairings.quote: “The anicham flower withers when smelt; a guest withers when the host's face turns cold.” மோப்பக் குழையும் அனிச்சம் முகந்திரிந்து நோக்கக் குழையும் விருந்து. Tirukkuṟaḷ 90

chapters.title: Customer Relationship Marketing
chapters.scope: Building lasting customer relationships: relationship marketing and CRM, one-to-one and permission marketing, retention and loyalty, and the CRM value chain.

blocks.title: Relationship marketing and CRM
blocks.html:
A kirana owner in Indore knows which families buy what, keeps their favourite brands in stock and gives regulars credit. A supermarket chain with lakhs of customers cannot remember faces, yet it wants the same loyalty.

In plain wordsRelationship marketing treats a customer as a long relationship to be looked after, not a single sale to be closed.

Exam definitionRelationship marketing is attracting, maintaining and, in multi-service organisations, enhancing customer relationships (Leonard Berry, 1983).

Berry introduced the term in 1983. Relationship marketing builds long-term ties with customers, employees and partners, rather than focusing on single transactions. Its aims are retention, long-term engagement, loyalty and higher profitability.

Strategy and system. Relationship marketing is the strategy: retention goals, public relations, marketing and advertising. Customer relationship management covers the operational tasks that support it.

AspectCustomer relationship marketing (CRMk)Customer relationship management (CRM)
What it isA strategy focused on long-term relationships rather than one-time salesA technology-driven system for managing customer interactions and data
ProvidesDirection: whom to keep and howA central customer database, personalised communication, better service

Kotler and Keller define customer relationship management as the process of carefully managing detailed information about individual customers and all customer touch points to maximise loyalty. A touch point is any occasion on which a customer meets the brand: marketing emails, service calls, website visits, store visits and loyalty programmes. A hotel's touch points include reservations, check-in and check-out, frequent-stay programmes, room service, business services, the gym, laundry, restaurants and bars. The internet has moved marketing from mass marketing to personalised marketing through email, websites, call centres and databases.

Thoughtful firms turn customers into clients. Customers may be nameless, served as part of a mass or segment by whoever is available. Clients cannot be nameless: the professional assigned to them serves them individually.

Why retention matters. Keeping customers usually costs less than winning new ones. Frederick Reichheld and W.
