Earl Sasser (1990) found that cutting customer defections by 5 per cent could raise profits by 25 to 85 per cent, depending on the industry. Churn is the rate at which customers leave. Customer lifetime value (CLV) is the present value of the profits a customer will bring over the whole relationship.

CLV, worked step by step (illustrative numbers). A family spends ₹3,000 a month at the kirana store, and the store keeps a 10% margin. That is ₹300 profit a month, or ₹3,600 a year. Suppose the family stays three more years, and money is discounted at 10% a year:

CLV = 3,600 ÷ 1.1 + 3,600 ÷ 1.1² + 3,600 ÷ 1.1³ = 3,273 + 2,975 + 2,705 ≈ ₹8,950

Undiscounted, the three years add up to ₹10,800. Discounting gives less, because a rupee earned later is worth less today. Losing this family over one billing error costs about ₹8,950, not one month's ₹300.

Don't confuse relationship marketing with CRM software. Relationship marketing (CRMk) is the strategy: which customers to keep, and how. CRM is the system that records data and touch points to carry the strategy out. A firm can buy the software and still treat every customer as a one-off sale.

Where it breaks. Not every customer wants a relationship; some buy on price each time and ignore loyalty offers. The 25 to 85 per cent range came from particular service industries, so it is not a rule for every firm. CLV rests on guesses about how long a customer will stay.

For exams. Know Berry (1983) for the term, Kotler and Keller's definition of CRM, Reichheld and Sasser's 5 per cent and 25 to 85 per cent, and the meaning of CLV, churn and touch points.

CRMk is the strategy; CRM is the technology.

blocks.title: One-to-one and permission marketing
blocks.html:
A bank sends the same credit-card offer to ten lakh customers, including people who already hold the card. Most delete it, and some unsubscribe from all its messages.

In plain wordsOne-to-one marketing treats each customer as a market of one; permission marketing speaks only to customers who have agreed to listen.

Exam definitionPermission marketing is the privilege, not the right, of delivering anticipated, personal and relevant messages to people who actually want to get them (Seth Godin).

One-to-one marketing (Don Peppers and Martha Rogers, The One to One Future, 1993) treats each customer as a segment of one. Their IDIC model has four steps. It suits complex products that need continuing engagement.

StepFocusA two-wheeler dealer in Lucknow (illustration)
IdentifyKnow each customer individually; build the customer databaseRecords each buyer, vehicle and service date
DifferentiateRank customers by their value (CLV) and their needsSpots families who own several vehicles and service them on time
InteractEngage customers in personalised, cost-efficient dialogueSends service reminders to customers who opted in
CustomiseTailor products, services and messages to each customerOffers an exchange deal when a bike reaches five years

In the IDIC model, firms spend proportionately more effort on their most valuable customers (MVCs). They find them by estimating customer lifetime value: the net present value of future profits from purchases, margins and referrals, less customer-specific service costs. One-to-one marketing suits firms that collect much individual data and sell many products. Those products can be cross-sold, need periodic replacement or upgrading, and are of high value. For other firms, the investment may exceed the payoff.

Permission marketing (Seth Godin, 1999) asks for the customer's consent before sending marketing messages. Communication then becomes anticipated, personal and relevant. It is the opposite of interruption marketing, which pushes messages at people who did not ask for them.

Participatory marketing. Permission marketing assumes consumers know what they want. When their preferences are vague or conflicting, participatory marketing may fit better: firm and consumer work out together how best to satisfy the consumer. Customers help to develop and promote products, acting as co-creators, advocates and content creators. Not every consumer wants to be involved with every brand, and even then only some of the time.

Reviews and recommendations. Recommendation by a relative or friend remains the strongest influence on choice. Online ratings and reviews matter more and more, and some stores display them. Firms court bloggers and influencers with large followings through samples and early information; such favours should be disclosed. Online retailers add their own recommendations. Kotler and Keller cite one estimate that recommendation systems contribute 10 to 30 per cent of an online retailer's sales.

Don't confuse permission marketing with one-to-one marketing. One-to-one marketing is about tailoring the offer to each customer. Permission marketing is about consent to be contacted at all. A firm can personalise a message that nobody agreed to receive; that is still interruption.

Where it breaks. One-to-one marketing needs rich data and many products to sell; a firm with one cheap product rarely recovers the cost. Permission is easy to lose: one irrelevant message too many, and customers withdraw it. Paid influencer praise misleads buyers when it is not disclosed.

For exams. Match Peppers and Rogers (1993) to one-to-one marketing and IDIC, and Godin (1999) to permission marketing. Know IDIC in order, and that interruption marketing is the opposite of permission marketing.

Identify, Differentiate, Interact, Customise.

blocks.title: Customer retention and loyalty
blocks.html:
A mobile shop in Jaipur wins about 100 new customers a month from a promotion, yet its customer list stays the same size. Customers are leaving as fast as they arrive.

In plain wordsCustomer retention is keeping the customers you already have, so they go on buying from you.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: the customer retention rate is the percentage of customers at the start of a period who are still customers at its end; churn is the percentage who leave.

The leaking bucket. Adding customers while losing others is like pouring water into a leaking bucket. Churn has common causes: poor service, unmet expectations, billing errors and complex processes.

Measuring it, step by step (illustrative numbers). A shop starts the year with 2,000 customers. By December, 300 of them have stopped buying.

Retention rate = (2,000 − 300) ÷ 2,000 = 85%; churn = 15%

New customers won during the year do not count, because the rate follows the starting group. At 85% a year, after three years 2,000 × 0.85³ ≈ 1,228 of them remain. At 90%, 2,000 × 0.9³ = 1,458 remain. After three years, five points of retention have kept 230 more customers.

Reducing defection. Measure the retention rate; find why customers leave and which causes the firm can manage; then compare a lost customer's lifetime value with the cost of keeping them.

Customer base management (Kotler and Keller) aims to:

  • reduce churn and increase the length of relationships;
  • raise each customer's value through share of wallet, cross-selling and up-selling;
  • make low-profit customers more profitable, or let them go;
  • give high-value customers disproportionate attention.

Customers can be segmented by loyalty, profitability and engagement. The marketing funnel (awareness, interest, purchase, loyalty) shows what share of the target market reaches each stage. The conversion rate between stages reveals bottlenecks, as when far fewer triers become repeat users.

In the funnel above, 40% of aware buyers try the atta. Only 15 ÷ 40 = 37.5% of triers buy again, and 8 ÷ 15 ≈ 53% of repeat buyers become loyal. The trial-to-repeat step is the bottleneck, so the firm checks the product and the price before spending more on awareness.

Three kinds of activity improve loyalty and retention:

  • Interacting with customers and listening to them.
  • Loyalty programmes: frequency programmes reward customers who buy often and in quantity; club membership programmes are open to all buyers, or to an affinity group or a fee-paying few.
  • Institutional ties, such as equipment or computer links that help customers manage orders, payroll and inventory.

Building loyalty. Leonard Berry and A. Parasuraman (1991) described three levels of relationship marketing, each binding the customer more tightly.

LevelHowExamples
Financial benefitsRewards that lower the customer's costDiscounts, cashback, frequency programmes
Social benefitsPersonal ties with staff and other customersExclusive events, communities, club memberships
Structural tiesLinks built into the customer's own systemsTechnology integration, customised solutions

Other loyalty builders: superior products and experiences, listening to the voice of the customer, easy complaint channels, and recognising employees who serve customers well.

Don't confuse cross-selling with up-selling. Cross-selling sells a related product: a bank sells a home-loan customer an insurance policy. Up-selling sells a higher-value version of the same thing: a premium account instead of a basic one.

Where it breaks. Financial rewards are the easiest level for rivals to copy; a bigger discount next door can undo them. A customer held only by points or switching costs is retained, but not truly loyal. Letting low-profit customers go can also hurt, if they bring referrals or later grow.

For exams. Expect Berry and Parasuraman's three levels in order, and a retention or churn calculation.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision (illustrative numbers). A gym in Pune has 1,000 members, each bringing ₹4,800 of profit a year. It loses 300 members a year. A one-off ₹6 lakh spent on better onboarding and follow-up calls is expected to cut this year's losses to 200. Is it worth it?

The 100 extra members kept bring 100 × ₹4,800 = ₹4.8 lakh in their first year, less than the ₹6 lakh cost. If each stays two years on average, they bring ₹9.6 lakh, and the spend pays. The answer turns on how long kept members stay, which is their lifetime value.

Links. Brand management (this unit) treats loyalty from the brand's side.

Financial, social, structural: each binds more tightly.

blocks.title: The CRM value chain and process
blocks.html:
A car dealership in Pune buys CRM software. A year later its salespeople still keep leads in their own notebooks, and the system holds little that is useful.

In plain wordsCRM done properly is a way of running the whole business around chosen customers, with software as one of its tools.

Exam definitionCRM is the core business strategy that integrates internal processes and functions, and external networks, to create and deliver value to targeted customers at a profit. It is grounded on high-quality customer-related data and enabled by information technology (Francis Buttle).

Francis Buttle's CRM value chain (2004) has five primary stages:

  • Customer portfolio analysis: which customers to serve.
  • Customer intimacy: knowing them.
  • Network development: with suppliers, partners and employees.
  • Value proposition development.
  • Managing the customer lifecycle: acquisition, retention and development.

They rest on four supporting conditions: leadership and culture, data and IT, people and processes.

The five-step CRM process is the operational sequence a sales and marketing team follows.

StepAim
1 Generate brand awarenessMake target customers know the brand
2 Acquire leadsDraw interested prospects into contact
3 Convert leads into customersTurn prospects into buyers
4 Provide quality customer supportKeep customers satisfied
5 Drive upsellingGrow each customer's value with higher-value or added products

At each step a different tool is used:

  • Marketing builds buyer personas, fictional profiles of ideal customers by demographics, interests, values and challenges, to target awareness campaigns.
  • Lead generation draws prospects into the sales funnel through sign-up forms, chat and content.
  • Lead scoring helps sales staff spot the prospects most likely to buy.
  • Support teams gather feedback after purchase, and upselling offers warranties or higher-featured products.

The dealership, in numbers (illustrative). It gets 400 leads a month, and 32 of them buy: a conversion rate of 32 ÷ 400 = 8%. With lead scoring, salespeople call the 100 highest-scored leads first. If 20 of those buy, that group converts at 20 ÷ 100 = 20%, so the team spends its time where sales are likeliest.

What CRM systems do. They record leads and contacts, and sort them into customers, lost customers, prospects, suppliers, partners and influencers. They track every interaction centrally, so all staff see the history. They reveal prospects not yet sold to, and keep customer data when staff move on.

Benefits: higher conversion rates; closer relationships; better business performance through cross-selling, up-selling and referrals; and higher employee productivity, by automating tasks such as email, lead scoring and pipeline management. Cloud-based CRM adds flexibility and access from anywhere.

Don't confuse the value chain with the five-step process. Buttle's value chain is a strategic model: five stages resting on four supports. The five-step process, from awareness to upselling, is a sales routine. Shorter versions of the value chain often leave out customer intimacy; Buttle's has five primary stages.

Where it breaks. Software fails without the supports: leaders who use it, staff trained to enter data, and processes built around it. Poor data gives poor lead scores. Holding more customer data also brings privacy duties, covered in Emerging trends in marketing (this unit).

For exams. Know Buttle's five stages and four supports, and the five process steps, in order.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. The Pune dealership asks why its CRM failed. Buttle's chain points first to the supports, not the software. Did the sales head use the system in reviews? Were staff trained, and was entering a lead made part of the daily routine?

The fix starts with leadership and process, such as weekly sales reviews run from the system. Only then does data build up for portfolio analysis and lead scoring.

Awareness, leads, conversion, support, upselling.

text: Berry and Parasuraman's first two levels bind customers by rewards and by personal ties. The Kuṟaḷ says that one who is generous in giving and speaks kindly will be surrounded by kin, ring upon ring. It describes how a person keeps relatives close, not how a firm keeps customers.
pairings.quote: “One who gives and speaks kindly will be surrounded by kin, ring upon ring.” கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின் அடுக்கிய சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப் படும். Tirukkuṟaḷ 525

pairings.classic: the thread that leaves a knot
text: Rahim warns against snapping the thread of affection: once broken it does not join, and if it is joined a knot remains. Retention work makes the same point about customers: winning back one who left costs more than keeping them, and the relationship rarely returns to what it was. Rahim wrote of personal bonds, so this is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Rahim, do not snap the thread of love with a jerk. Once broken it will not join again, and if it does, a knot remains.” रहिमन धागा प्रेम का, मत तोड़ो चटकाय । टूटे से फिर ना मिले, मिले गाँठ परि जाय ॥ rahiman dhāgā prem kā, mat toṛo chaṭkāy; ṭūṭe se phir nā mile, mile gā̃ṭh pari jāy. Rahīm, dohā (Hindi)

chapters.title: Retail Marketing
chapters.scope: What retailers do, the kinds of store and non-store retailers, how retailers organise, and recent trends in Indian and world retail.

blocks.title: Retailing and store retailers
blocks.html:
A biscuit factory in Pune can make a lakh packets a day, yet families buy them one packet at a time, at a shop near home. The business that makes that last sale is the retailer.

In plain wordsRetailing is selling to people who will use the product themselves, not resell it or use it in a business.

Exam definitionRetailing includes all the activities involved in selling goods or services directly to final consumers for their personal, non-business use (Kotler and Keller).

The retailer is the final link in the distribution channel. It connects manufacturers with consumers, creates satisfaction at the point of sale, and passes customer feedback back up the chain.

A retailer is any business whose sales come mainly from retailing. But any organisation that sells to final consumers is doing retailing, whether it is a manufacturer, a wholesaler or a retailer. The method does not matter (in person, by mail, phone, vending machine or online), nor the place (a store, the street or the buyer's home). A shoe maker's factory outlet is retailing, though the firm is a manufacturer.

Kotler and Armstrong classify store retailers on four bases: the amount of service, the product line sold, relative prices, and how they are organised. Supermarkets are classified by product line.

Service levelFeature
Self-serviceCustomers serve themselves; lowest prices
Self-selectionCustomers shop on their own, with help available
Limited serviceMore help, credit and returns, and knowledgeable staff
Full serviceSalespeople help throughout; premium stores

The more service a store gives, the more it costs to run, so prices usually rise from self-service to full service.

TypeDescription
Specialty storeA narrow but deep product line, with expert advice
Department storeSeveral product lines, each run as a separate department
SupermarketA large, low-cost, low-margin, high-volume, self-service store for groceries and household products
Convenience storeA small store near homes, open long hours, selling a limited line of fast-moving goods
Drug store (pharmacy)Medicines and health products, sometimes with clinics
Discount storeStandard goods at lower prices, accepting lower margins for higher volume
Hard discounterA limited assortment at very low prices
Off-price retailerLeftover, surplus or irregular branded goods below regular prices, as in factory outlets
SuperstoreA very large store for routinely bought food and non-food items, with services; includes category killers, which carry a deep assortment in one line
Catalogue showroomA broad selection of discounted branded goods, ordered from a catalogue

Why low margins can pay. Take two grocery stores in one town (illustrative numbers). A full-service store sells ₹1 lakh a day at a 20% gross margin, which leaves ₹20,000. A supermarket sells ₹4 lakh a day at an 8% margin, which leaves ₹32,000. The lower margin earns more rupees because volume is four times higher. The supermarket also carries higher rent and wage bills, so volume must stay high.

Don't confuse an off-price retailer with a discount store. A discount store sells regular, standard goods cheaply by accepting a lower margin. An off-price retailer sells leftover, surplus or irregular branded goods, bought below regular prices. In the same way, a category killer is not a specialty store: both go deep in one line, but the category killer is a superstore.

Where it breaks. Real stores mix types. A neighbourhood kirana is a convenience store by size and hours, but it gives limited service: credit to regular customers and home delivery. Most Indian retail still happens in small independent shops like this, which a Western list of formats fits only loosely.

For exams. Expect a description to match with a store type, and the four bases of classification. Remember the service ladder in order: self-service, self-selection, limited service, full service.

By service, by product line, by price, by organisation.

blocks.title: Non-store and corporate retailing
blocks.html:
A kirana owner pays more for a carton of soap than the chain supermarket down the road, because the chain buys for many stores at once. Corporate retailing is about getting that kind of buying power.

In plain wordsNon-store retailing sells without a shop. Corporate retailing is shops that buy, brand or sell as a group rather than alone.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: non-store retailing is selling to final consumers through direct selling, direct marketing, automatic vending and buying services. Corporate retailing covers chains, voluntary chains, cooperatives, franchises and merchandising conglomerates.

Selling without a store. Four forms are named in the exam texts.

FormHow it works
Direct sellingPersonal selling at home or work, including multi-level marketing
Direct marketingMail, telemarketing, TV shopping and the internet
Automatic vendingUnmanned machines selling around the clock; convenience and impulse goods
Buying serviceServes a specific clientele, often employees of large organisations, who get discounts from selected retailers

How retailers organise. The forms differ in who owns the outlets and who organises the joint buying.

FormDescription
Corporate chainTwo or more outlets under common ownership and control, with central buying and merchandising
Voluntary chainIndependent retailers organised by a wholesaler for group buying and common merchandising
Retailer cooperativeIndependent retailers who set up a central buying organisation and run joint promotions
Consumer cooperativeA retail firm owned by its customers, who contribute capital, vote on policy, elect managers and receive dividends; Mumbai's Apna Bazar is an example
Franchise organisationA contractual system in which franchisees run outlets under the franchisor's brand and system, for a fee
Merchandising conglomerateA corporation owning several diversified retail brands and formats

Corporate retail organisations gain economies of scale, greater buying power, wider brand recognition and better-trained staff than independent stores usually can.

Private labels (also called reseller, store, house or distributor brands) are a retailer's own brands, as Marks & Spencer, Benetton and The Body Shop sell. They give the retailer more control over price and quality, higher margins and stronger customer loyalty. An illustration: a store buys a branded pack of biscuits for ₹80 and sells it for ₹100, a margin of ₹20 (20% of price). It has its own label made for ₹60 and sells it for ₹90, a margin of ₹30 (33% of price). The shopper pays less and the store earns more per pack.

Don't confuse a voluntary chain with a retailer cooperative. Both give independent shops group buying. A wholesaler organises a voluntary chain; in a retailer cooperative the retailers set up the buying body themselves. Study notes sometimes give Lijjat Papad as a consumer cooperative. In fact it is a cooperative of the women who make its products, not one owned by its customers. Direct selling also differs from direct marketing: direct selling uses a salesperson in person, direct marketing reaches buyers through media.

Where it breaks. Multi-level marketing can slide into a pyramid scheme, where income comes from recruiting people rather than selling to consumers; Indian law prohibits such schemes. Franchisees give up much of their freedom, and one badly run outlet harms the whole brand. With a private label, the retailer, not a manufacturer, answers for quality.

For exams. Match each form to who owns or organises it. The consumer cooperative is the only one owned by its customers.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. A bakery in Pune runs three successful shops and wants thirty. Opening its own outlets keeps full control of recipes and service, but needs capital it does not have. Franchising lets franchisees put in the money and grows faster, but the bakery must write down its system, train others, and inspect them. The question to settle first is whether the bakery's quality can be written into a manual. If it lives in one head baker's hands, franchising will dilute it.

Links. Chains, voluntary chains, cooperatives and franchises are vertical marketing systems, covered in Distribution (this unit). Franchising abroad is a form of licensing, one of the modes of entry in International marketing. Private labels raise the brand decisions covered in Brand management.

Chain, voluntary chain, cooperative, franchise, conglomerate.

blocks.title: Trends in Indian and world retail
blocks.html:
A kirana owner in Nagpur now takes UPI payments, delivers phone orders and stocks brands his father never sold. The retail trends below explain why his shop, and the mall across town, keep changing.

In plain wordsOrganised retail is retail by registered businesses, usually chains with systems and trained staff. Unorganised retail is small owner-run shops and street vendors.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: organised retailing is trading by licensed retailers registered for taxes, such as hypermarkets and retail chains. Unorganised retailing is traditional low-cost formats such as kirana shops, owner-run general stores, and handcart and pavement vendors.

Trends in India. Most of these push retail toward organised, digital formats, while the kirana adapts rather than disappears.

TrendWhat is happening
Demographic changeDual-income and nuclear families with more discretionary spending
Convenience shoppingMalls and organised retail offering one-stop shopping
Online retailRapid growth of e-commerce as internet use spreads
TechnologyBarcode scanners, CCTV, digital signage and retail automation
Digital paymentsCards, UPI and digital wallets reducing cash use
ExpansionGrowth into Tier-II and Tier-III cities
Kirana modernisationNeighbourhood stores adding self-service, home delivery, credit and digital ordering
PartnershipsAlliances and joint ventures that share investment and risk
Government policyFDI rules: 100 per cent in single-brand retail through the automatic route since 2018; up to 51 per cent in multi-brand retail with government approval since 2012
Smarter consumersResearching products online before buying

Wider trends. These apply to retailing worldwide, India included.

TrendWhat is happening
New retail forms and combinationsBookshops with cafés, fuel stations with food stores, bank branches and services inside malls
Intertype competitionDiscount stores, catalogue showrooms and department stores all compete for the same buyers with the same merchandise
Store against non-store retailingDirect mail, TV, phones and the internet take business from stores, which answer with their own websites and more engaging in-store experiences
Giant retailersSuperior information systems, logistics and buying power let large chains offer good service and huge volumes at appealing prices
Investment in technologyBetter forecasts, inventory control, electronic ordering, and in-store screens
Global retailersRetailers with distinctive formats and strong positioning, such as IKEA and Apple, expand abroad
Shopper marketingKotler and Keller report an estimate that 70 to 80 per cent of purchase decisions are made in the store, so firms work to influence buyers at the point of purchase
Store design and entertainmentLayouts that draw people in, keep them longer and encourage impulse buying; food courts, cinemas, play areas and cafés

Intertype competition means competition between different kinds of store. A supermarket, a kirana and an online seller all compete for the same family's monthly grocery list.

Don't confuse single-brand with multi-brand retail FDI. Single-brand retail is a firm selling only its own brand in its stores; foreign firms may own all of it through the automatic route, with no prior government approval. Multi-brand retail is a store selling many brands, like a supermarket; foreign ownership is capped at 51 per cent and needs government approval.

Where it breaks. In India, buying behaviour is far from uniform across income groups. Organised retail has made less impact on lower-income shoppers, and small independent retailers survive by offering personal service, credit and nearness. Organised retail needs trained staff, and technology gives it cost and service advantages over unorganised players. FDI rules are policy, and policy changes, so check the current position before relying on it.

For exams. The FDI limits, routes and years are the most-asked facts. Also expect a trend to match with its description, such as kirana modernisation or expansion into smaller cities.

Organised, online, digital and reaching smaller towns.

pairings.modern: Trust at the point of sale
text: The Arthaśāstra appoints a superintendent of weights and measures to make and stamp the standard ones, and in Book 4 fines traders who cheat buyers with false weights and measures. A retailer's business still rests on that trust at the point of sale.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.19; traders at 4.2

chapters.title: International Marketing
chapters.scope: Why firms go abroad, how they choose and enter foreign markets, and the steps of the global marketing process.

blocks.title: Going international
blocks.html:
An auto-parts maker in Pune finds orders flat at home, while a buyer in Germany asks for a quote. Selling abroad looks like easy growth, but it brings a new currency, new rules and customers who want different things.

In plain wordsInternational marketing is marketing in more than one country, adjusting to each country's customers, rules and culture.

Exam definitionInternational marketing is the performance of business activities designed to plan, price, promote and direct the flow of a company's goods and services to consumers or users in more than one nation for a profit (Cateora and Graham).

It applies the same marketing principles across national borders. Global leaders such as Coca-Cola, Samsung, Honda and Sony draw on advantages in R&D, scale, global logistics, marketing expertise and finance. Supply chains are global too. Kotler and Keller's example is Otis Elevator, which drew door systems from France, gears from Spain, electronics from Germany and motors from Japan, with systems integration in the United States.

Why go internationalRisks
Higher market growthDifferent customer preferences
Economies of scaleCultural differences
Spreading risk across marketsRegulatory complexity
Competitive advantagePolitical and economic instability
Serving existing customers who have gone globalCurrency fluctuations

Going abroad in stages. Most firms do not start by building a factory abroad. They move step by step, and commitment and risk rise at each step.

StageDescription
1No regular export activity: domestic operations only
2Exports through independent agents
3Export department and sales subsidiaries abroad
4Production and marketing facilities abroad

This stepwise pattern follows the Uppsala studies of Swedish firms (Jan Johanson and Finn Wiedersheim-Paul, 1975). For the Pune firm, an illustration: it first ships through an export agent (stage 2). As orders grow, it sets up an export department and a sales office in Germany (stage 3). Years later it may build a plant there (stage 4).

The global marketing process runs in five steps, whatever the stage.

In step 3 the firm decides how far to standardise its marketing mix, keeping it the same in every country, or to adapt it to each one. Standardising saves cost; adapting fits local tastes, rules and incomes.

Don't confuse international marketing with exporting. Exporting is one way to enter a market. International marketing is the whole job: choosing markets, choosing how to enter, and adapting the product, price, promotion and distribution for each.

Where it breaks. The stages describe many firms, not all. Software and online businesses often sell abroad from their first years; researchers call them born globals. Other firms skip stages by buying a foreign company outright.

For exams. Know the four stages in order, the Uppsala link (Johanson and Wiedersheim-Paul, 1975), and the five steps of the global marketing process.

Go deeper for practitioners

Why stages happen. The Uppsala model explains the steps by learning. A firm knows little about a foreign market, so it commits a little. As it learns, uncertainty falls and it commits more. Jan Johanson and Jan-Erik Vahlne set this out as a model in 1977, and later revised it to stress business networks.

A decision. The Pune firm's German buyer wants a supplier with local stock and service. An agent cannot give that. The firm must judge whether German orders are steady enough to pay for a sales office, or whether it should wait a year and learn more through the agent.

Links. International strategies, such as multidomestic, global and transnational, are covered in Cooperative, international and retrenchment strategies (Unit 6).

Domestic, agents, subsidiaries, production abroad.

blocks.title: Selecting foreign markets
blocks.html:
A Kolhapur footwear maker can afford to enter one or two countries this year, not twenty. Which ones, and in what order?

In plain wordsPsychic distance is how foreign a market feels to a firm: different language, culture, laws and ways of doing business.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: psychic distance is the set of factors that prevent or disturb the flow of information between a firm and a market, such as differences in language, culture, political systems, education and industrial development.

Firms weigh four things: product suitability, geographic proximity, economic potential and political stability. Many prefer psychic proximity: countries with a similar language, culture and legal system. US firms, for example, have often entered Canada, the UK and Australia first.

Scoring the choices. A simple way to compare markets is to score each from 1 to 5 on the four criteria and weight them. An illustration with three unnamed countries:

Criterion (weight)Country ACountry BCountry C
Product suitability (30%)435
Proximity, geographic and psychic (20%)523
Economic potential (30%)354
Political stability (20%)432
Weighted score3.93.43.7

Country A: 4 × 0.3 + 5 × 0.2 + 3 × 0.3 + 4 × 0.2 = 1.2 + 1.0 + 0.9 + 0.8 = 3.9. Country B: 0.9 + 0.4 + 1.5 + 0.6 = 3.4. Country C: 1.5 + 0.6 + 1.2 + 0.4 = 3.7. The near, familiar market A wins, although B has the largest economic potential.

In what order. Once the list is chosen, the firm decides whether to enter one country at a time or many at once.

AspectWaterfallSprinkler
EntryCountry by country, in sequenceMany countries at once
Risk and investmentLower; learning from each marketHigher investment
AdvantageControlled expansion and learningFirst-mover advantage before rivals copy
ExamplesBMW, General ElectricMicrosoft's simultaneous worldwide launch of Windows

Emerging markets, notably the BRICS economies, offer untapped demand, high growth and an expanding middle class. The acronym stands for Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa; the group has since admitted more members. Winning there calls for affordable prices, adapted products and local marketing. Unilever's small, affordable sachets and Colgate-Palmolive's video vans touring rural India are the textbook examples.

Don't confuse psychic distance with geographic distance. Geographic distance is kilometres. Psychic distance is how different the market feels. A far country can be psychically close, as the UK and Australia are for US firms, and a neighbour can be psychically distant.

Where it breaks. Scores and weights are judgements, and changing a weight can change the winner. Psychic proximity can also mislead. A market that feels similar can lead a firm to underestimate the real differences; researchers have called this the psychic distance paradox. A sprinkler launch works only when the firm can afford to support every market at once.

For exams. Know the four criteria, psychic proximity, and the waterfall and sprinkler approaches with their examples.

Similar markets first, or many at once.

blocks.title: Modes of entry
blocks.html:
The Pune auto-parts maker now has steady buyers in Germany. It can ship through an export house, run its own exports, license its design, form a joint venture, or build a plant. Each option puts more at stake and gives more say.

In plain wordsAn entry mode is the way a firm gets its product, know-how or brand into a foreign market.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: an entry mode is an institutional arrangement that makes possible the entry of a company's products, technology, human skills, management or other resources into a foreign country.

Kotler and Keller arrange entry modes in order of increasing commitment, risk, control and profit potential.

ModeHow it worksInvestmentRiskControl
Indirect exportingSelling through independent intermediaries at homeLowLowLow
Direct exportingThe company handles its own exports, through its own export department, branches or agentsMediumMediumHigher
LicensingA foreign firm gets the right to use a process, trademark or patent for a royalty; also management contracts, contract manufacturing and franchising (as Marriott, Hyatt and McDonald's use)LowLowLow; the licensee may become a competitor
Joint venturePartnership with local firms sharing ownership, risk and profitMediumSharedShared
Direct investment (FDI)Building or buying production facilities abroadVery highHighFull

Licensing against a plant, in rupees (illustrative numbers). Suppose a German licensee sells ₹10 crore a year of parts made to the Pune firm's design and pays a 5% royalty. The firm earns ₹10 crore × 5% = ₹50 lakh a year, with almost no investment. Alternatively, the firm builds its own plant for ₹20 crore. If the plant makes a profit of ₹2 crore a year on the same sales, the firm earns four times as much (₹2 crore ÷ ₹50 lakh = 4). But it needs ten years of profit to get its ₹20 crore back (₹20 crore ÷ ₹2 crore), and it carries all the risk.

Joint ventures bring local expertise, shared resources and easier government approval, and have been common in China and India. FDI gives full control, lower production cost in some markets, a strong local image and better market access.

Don't confuse licensing with franchising. A licence gives the right to use one asset, such as a patent, process or trademark. A franchise is a fuller form of licensing: the franchisee gets the brand and the whole way of running the business, and must follow it.

Where it breaks. The order is a broad rule, and licensing breaks it: it sits third, yet the table shows low investment and low control. Joint ventures often run into disputes between partners over control, profits and strategy. Direct investment exposes the firm to political and currency risk in a country it cannot leave cheaply.

For exams. Know the five modes in order, and the trade-off: more control and profit potential come with more investment and risk.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. The Pune firm's design is its main advantage. Licensing earns money fast but teaches a German firm how to make the part; in a few years that firm could compete. A joint venture with a German distributor gives local knowledge and shares the cost, but the partners must agree on prices and profits. A plant gives full control at the highest risk. The first question is how easily the design could be copied: the easier, the stronger the case for keeping control.

Links. The stages of internationalisation in Going international follow the same rising order of commitment. Franchising in retail is covered in Retail marketing (this unit).

Export, license, joint venture, invest: more commitment, more control.

text: The Arthaśāstra's director of trade, for trade in a foreign land, is to compare the price and value of the goods to be exchanged, and to reckon the duties, road cess, escort charges, ferry dues and other costs before judging the profit; he should also seek the friendship of officials along the way. That is a foreign-market assessment of cost, price and access before entry.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.16

text: Market selection comes before entry. The Kuṟaḷ says to begin no undertaking and to despise no enemy until one has seen the place from which to act. It is military advice about ground, not about countries as markets.
pairings.quote: “Begin no undertaking and scorn no foe until you have found the place to act from.” தொடங்கற்க எவ்வினையும் எள்ளற்க முற்றும் இடங்கண்ட பின்அல் லது. Tirukkuṟaḷ 491

chapters.title: Emerging Trends in Marketing
chapters.scope: Social and green marketing, online, digital and direct marketing, rural marketing, and unconventional tactics such as guerrilla and roadblock marketing.

blocks.title: Social marketing and green marketing
blocks.html:
Social marketing applies commercial marketing techniques to influence behaviour that benefits individuals and society. Philip Kotler and Gerald Zaltman introduced the idea in 1971. Its key components are a target audience, a desired behaviour change, exchange theory (the change must offer benefits that outweigh its perceived costs) and a marketing mix. India's pulse polio and Swachh Bharat campaigns are examples.

ObjectivesBehaviour change, community development, public participation, social welfare
StrategiesMedia and social media campaigns, community engagement, partnerships with NGOs and government
ChallengesCultural sensitivity; measuring long-term impact

Green marketing markets environmentally sustainable products and practices: eco-friendly products, sustainable processes, eco-labelling and green advertising. Its aims are to promote eco-friendly consumption and build a responsible brand image; its tools include transparency, CSR initiatives and attention to the whole product life cycle. Its main risk is greenwashing: false or exaggerated environmental claims, which breed consumer scepticism. Green products may also cost more to make.

Sell behaviour change for society; sell sustainability honestly.

blocks.title: Green marketing in practice
blocks.html:
Green marketing promotes products on the strength of their environmental advantages, through product changes, cleaner processes, sustainable packaging and green advertising, so as to reduce the harm a product does in its making, use and disposal. A green product allows economic development while conserving resources for future generations: it neither pollutes the earth nor depletes natural resources, and it can be recycled or conserved. Companies look at three things: the raw materials, the product itself, and its packaging.

Objectives: to meet corporate social responsibility, reduce costs, show how environment-friendly the offering is, communicate the brand message, and adopt sustainable, socially accountable practices. Benefits for the business: competitive advantage as consumers grow more aware, lower operating costs (natural light, water conservation, recycling), and a positive brand image that attracts talent and investors.

PGreen approach
ProductDesigned to use fewer resources, cause no pollution and be reusable or recyclable
PriceBuyers pay a premium only when they see added value, such as better performance, design or health benefits
PromotionAdvertising that links the product to the environment, promotes a green lifestyle, or presents a green corporate image
PlaceMaking green products available where and how buyers can get them, which strongly affects who buys

Practices: recycled and renewable materials, green energy (solar, wind, geothermal), less or eco-friendly packaging, avoiding toxic materials, and reusable, recyclable products. Strategies: green design, green positioning, green pricing, and green disposal systems for what the product leaves behind.

PrincipleMeaning
Consumer-oriented marketingSee marketing activities from the consumer's point of view
Customer-value marketingPut resources into building real customer value
Innovative marketingKeep seeking real improvements in products and marketing
Sense-of-mission marketingDefine the mission in broad social terms rather than narrow product terms
Societal marketingWeigh consumers' wants, the company's needs, consumers' long-term interests and society's interests

These are often presented as principles of green marketing; they are Kotler and Armstrong's principles of sustainable marketing, which green marketing applies. Greenwashing, claiming green habits a firm does not practise, misleads buyers and erodes trust.

Green product, price, place and promotion; green design, positioning, pricing and disposal.

blocks.title: Online and direct marketing
blocks.html:
Online (digital) marketing uses digital platforms for targeted, measurable and scalable customer engagement, aiming at brand awareness, website traffic, conversion and engagement.

ComponentPurpose
Search engine optimisation (SEO)Improve search rankings
Content marketingBlogs, videos and e-books that attract and inform
Social media marketingCustomer engagement
Email marketingPersonalised communication
Pay-per-click (PPC) advertisingPaid clicks and traffic

Strategies include inbound marketing (drawing customers with useful content), affiliate marketing and influencer marketing. In performance marketing advertisers pay only when a measurable action, such as a click, lead or sale, occurs. Challenges include data privacy (in India, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023), ad blockers and changing algorithms.

Direct marketing is one-to-one communication designed to get an immediate, measurable response: direct mail, telemarketing, email, catalogues and direct-response advertising. It relies on personalisation, a strong call to action, and tracking response and return on investment; its challenges are intrusiveness, managing the customer database and complying with regulations.

Targeted, measurable and paid for by results.

blocks.title: Digital marketing
blocks.html:
TermScope
Internet marketingUsing the internet to win customers, mainly through a website, search engine optimisation and pay-per-click ads, and converting that traffic into sales
E-marketingInternet marketing plus relationship building: email, online reviews, referral programmes, social media and CRM
Digital marketingThe widest term: all marketing through digital interfaces, online or not, including mobile apps and push notifications, in-app ads, electronic billboards and digital databases

Unlike traditional marketing, which is largely one-way, digital marketing allows two-way communication, and it reaches people where they spend more and more of their time: on screens.

MethodWhat it is
Search engine marketing (SEM)Paid advertising to raise visibility in search results, often used with SEO
Affiliate marketingPerformance-based revenue sharing, paying affiliates per sale made through their referral
Native advertisingPaid content that blends into the medium around it, such as sponsored articles; it should be clearly labelled ‘sponsored’ or ‘promoted’
Marketing automationSoftware that schedules social media posts, runs lead-nurturing email workflows and tracks campaigns

Benefits: global reach, a low cost of entry, measurable return on investment, precise targeting, the flexibility to change course quickly, an immediate connection with buyers who research online, relationship building through social media, and easy conversion, since a buyer can act at once.

Budgets scale with the firm: basic (websites, blogs and social media for start-ups), intermediate (adding SEO, SEM, PPC and email for medium firms) and advanced (comprehensive, often global, strategies for large firms). Building a strategy: identify marketing goals, settle the digital sales process, define target customers and buyer personas, choose channels, set clear benchmarks, and adjust as results come in.

Goals, sales process, personas, channels, benchmarks, adjustment.

blocks.title: Rural marketing
blocks.html:
Rural marketing designs strategies for rural consumers: penetrating rural markets, meeting local needs and helping raise living standards. It needs efficient distribution, affordable prices (small packs and sachets), products adapted to rural conditions, and promotion in local languages.

Indian practitioners often frame rural marketing in four As: availability, affordability, acceptability and awareness. Strategies use local opinion leaders, weekly markets (haats), agriculture-linked marketing, folk media and street campaigns. Challenges are logistics, poor infrastructure and cultural and linguistic diversity.

Available, affordable, acceptable, known.

blocks.title: Guerrilla and roadblock marketing
blocks.html:
AspectGuerrilla marketingRoadblock marketing
IdeaCreative, unconventional, low-cost tactics that surprise people and create buzz (Jay Conrad Levinson, Guerrilla Marketing, 1984)Advertising on many channels at the same time, so the audience meets the message wherever it turns
ObjectivesAttention, viral publicity, brand recallMaximum reach, high recall, strong visibility
TacticsStreet marketing, viral campaigns, experiential marketingPrime-time TV roadblocks, digital and radio roadblocks, coordinated media buying
ChallengesLegal permissions, ethical concerns, hard-to-measure returnsHigh cost, keeping the message consistent, ad fatigue

Guerrilla surprises cheaply; roadblock saturates expensively.

pairings.classic: what is taken, may it grow back
text: Green marketing asks that consumption leave the earth able to renew itself. The Atharvaveda's hymn to the Earth prays that what is dug from her may quickly grow again, and that her vitals and heart not be wounded. It is a prayer, not a policy, but it states the idea of renewal plainly.
pairings.quote: यत्ते भूमे विखनामि क्षिप्रं तदपि रोहतु । yat te bhūme vikhanāmi kṣipraṃ tad api rohatu. “What I dig from you, O Earth, may that quickly grow again.” Atharvaveda 12.1.35

text: Greenwashing wins sales with false claims. The Kuṟaḷ says that wealth gained by deceit and kept is like water poured into an unbaked clay pot: it will not hold. It speaks of deceit in general, not of environmental claims.
pairings.quote: “Guarding wealth gained by deceit is like keeping water in a pot of unbaked clay.” சலத்தால் பொருள்செய்தே மார்த்தல் பசுமண் கலத்துள்நீர் பெய்திரீஇ யற்று. Tirukkuṟaḷ 660

text: Rural marketing starts from the size and importance of the farm economy. The Kuṟaḷ says that however the world turns, it follows the plough, and so farming, though hard, is foremost. It praises agriculture; it does not speak of markets.
pairings.quote: “However it wanders, the world follows the plough; so farming, though toilsome, is foremost.” சுழன்றும்ஏர்ப் பின்னது உலகம் அதனால் உழந்தும் உழவே தலை. Tirukkuṟaḷ 1031
